title: Grain giant's $400m rail upgrade sparks unexpected train pain for country town
text:
Residents of a small country town say a decision by Western Australia's largest grain handler to upgrade its rail fleet is starting to rattle their homes and businesses to pieces.

With the state's rail network critical to transporting the millions of tonnes of grain harvested across WA's agricultural regions each year, Co-Operative Bulk Handling (CBH) has recently upgraded its rail fleet, with 17 new locomotives and 650 wagons.

But the move has sparked turmoil in Mount Barker, about 360 km south-east of Perth, where a busy rail route runs directly through the centre of town and residents previously considered the rumbling of trains an essential part of rural life.

Residents say the old trains, pictured here, were not as loud. (Supplied CBH)

Alexandra Spargo has lived about a kilometre from the tracks for the last four years, but in the past few weeks has noticed a change.

Ms Spargo believes the vibrations have cracked fresh paint in her recently renovated cottage.

"I never used to get woken up by the train and just recently I'm finding that I am and it's a lot louder than what the trains used to be before," she said.

" It's all newly painted … And I've just noticed I've got this long crack in the ceiling now, right at the front where the windows are. "

While conceding she cannot be certain, the location of the crack above her "rattling" windows makes her think the trains' vibrations are the cause.

Residents, some living as far as 5 kilometres from the tracks, have reported being woken in the night by the rumblings, or mistaking them for an earthquake.

Alexandra Spargo believes the trains' intense vibrations have caused cracks in her ceiling. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

Concerns over damage

For those closer to the train line, like antique dealer Mandy Dennis, there are fears for the long-term structural impact to the town's heritage buildings.

Her own shop is housed in a building more than 100 years old, and filled with precious antiques, which she now worries about every time a train rolls through.

"About a month ago, I was behind the counter … and all of a sudden the ground started vibrating," she said.

" It's never happened before, but all the crystal and the glasses started to clink and shake. "

Mandy Dennis says her antiques rattle when the trains go by. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

Ms Dennis's main concern is whether CBH would compensate her for any loss.

"We don't want the trains to go away," she said.

"But it would be good to know that if in future if there is an issue with breakages and the noises affecting the business in any way, or the structure, that CBH will take responsibility."

Len Handasyde says residents should continue engaging with CBH if they have concerns. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

Of the half-dozen residents who spoke to the ABC, nearly all expressed support for the rail network.

"What we need to understand is that rail is really important to us," Shire of Plantagenet president Len Handasyde said.

" For every train that goes through, it saves many, many trucks on their roads and it's a very efficient way to transport stuff. "

In a statement to the ABC, a CBH spokesperson said it was aware of residents reporting "different noise and vibration".

The spokesperson said the group was working with rail freight operator Aurizon and rail infrastructure manager Arc Infrastructure to investigate the issue.

The spokesperson said train operation, local track conditions and weather could be factors behind the noise and vibration.

Minister for Transport Rita Saffioti, Minister for Agriculture Jackie Jarvis, CBH Group chair Simon Stead, and CBH Group chief executive Ben Macnamara at the launch of CBH's new fleet in Forrestfield on Friday. (ABC Great Southern: Kate Forrester)

Complaints taint major milestone

The backlash has tainted an otherwise major milestone for CBH, which has spent more than $400 million on its new fleet — the largest in the co-operative's 93-year history.

On Friday, chair Simon Stead and chief executive Ben Macnamara officially launched the investment at the company's Metro Grain Centre in Forrestfield, flanked by two state ministers.

The new CM20ACi narrow-gauge locomotives are now in operation. (ABC Great Southern: Kate Forrester)

The doubling of the fleet will allow CBH to keep pace with the state's burgeoning grain production, which reached a record 27.35 million tonnes in 2025.

More than 90 per cent is exported, hence the pressure to optimise its passage to the nearest port.

title: 'Fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW' after Swans players allegation
text:
As the fallout continues with focus on the Sydney Swans men's AFL team, the club's women's team has been thrust into an unfair spotlight and become another unwilling casualty.

This was a week where the Swans AFLW team was being given equal billing to men with a double-header on the SCG, at a club that is very public in celebrating its inclusive values.

Swans players issue apology Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology.

Instead, the club's respect for women has been brought into question, with the women's players and women in the football community left feeling hurt and angry by the actions of the men's players.

The club has suspended five of its men's players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — for the remainder of the 2026 season for breaching club behavioural standards.

The five players are linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that they are being accused of sexual assault, and no-one has been arrested or charged in relation to the alleged incident.

Sympathies across the footy space remain first and foremost with the alleged victim, including with everyone spoken to for this story.

While finding it difficult to talk about anyone outside of the woman at the centre of this story, AFLW pioneer Chyloe Kurdas told ABC Sport it had been a "horrendous" week for many women in the footy space.

Sydney started its season on a high after a round one victory against Adelaide. (Getty: Mark Brake)

"As women, we live with the fear of sexual assault every day, and so this is not just something that only the Swans AFLW team will be feeling. There will be a fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW system," Kurdas said.

Diversity and inclusion leader Rana Hussain, who has worked across multiple sports including within AFL clubs, said sexual violence was not an abstract issue for women, as many were feeling this story deeply.

In Australia, one in five women have experienced sexual violence over the age of 15, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and Hussain said "even for those who haven't, most women understand its prevalence and have spent their lives learning to navigate and mitigate that risk".

"So these players are likely carrying this both as employees of the Sydney Swans and as women. And now they have to pull on the jumper, represent their club and potentially answer questions about something they had absolutely nothing to do with," Hussain said.

"We need to be really careful that the women of the Sydney Swans aren't asked to carry the cultural and emotional labour of this moment.

"Too often when these issues arise, women are leaned on to explain why it matters, what respectful culture should look like and what needs to change.

"They can love their club and represent it proudly while still asking difficult questions of their leaders about what the club's values actually mean when they are tested. Standing the players down is an important first step, but for the people inside that organisation, the work doesn't end there."

Sydney Swans will be put under an unwanted spotlight this weekend. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The ABC has spoken to sources in and around the AFLW program, who are not able to speak on the record, but conveyed their deep hurt.

One source close to the women's program said there were strong feelings of hurt, anger and humiliation following the actions from the men's players.

The double-header between the programs is the first in the club's history, with the women running out on the SCG for the first time for premiership points on Sunday before the men's game.

While the club will continue to build enthusiasm for the AFLW game against Essendon, the Swans players will have an undesired added layer of attention in what was originally a celebration.

Swans women's players and coaches are yet to publicly comment on the matter. However, that will likely change when they are obliged to do media post-game on Sunday.

Star player Chloe Molloy has already been questioned by media on her way into Swans HQ this week.

"The women, through no fault of their own, there'll be a spotlight put on them because of poor behaviour from men," Kurdas said.

Swans say players 'in serious breach' The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly linked to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

"We don't know what allegedly has happened. But running out there, flying Sydney Swans' flag and playing your role for the club, when you don't know if the boys that play would have your back and play their role for you?"

At a press conference on Wednesday, Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich said his club's women's team was "deeply disappointed" in the five male players suspended for breaches of club standards and that the club was "supporting them as best they can".

Earlier this week, former AFLW All Australian and now commentator for Seven and Triple M Kate McCarthy questioned how much the AFL space was doing to truly engage and include women and girls in footy spaces safely.

The post was praised by current AFLW players, including GWS' Tilly Lucas-Rodd, while Lions star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

In a lengthy post, McCarthy wrote in part: "The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates.

"It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise."

title: De Minaur suffers US Open seeding blow after Cincinatti boilover
text:
Alex de Minaur has missed out on a top-four US Open seeding after crashing out in the fourth round of the Cincinnati Masters.

De Minaur had the chance to climb into the world's top five with a deep run at the final Masters 1000 event before the season's last grand slam in New York.

But the Australian number one delivered a flat performance to fall 6-3, 6-4 to rising Frenchman Arthur Fils in just 82 minutes on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

De Minaur dropped serve once in each set and was unable to break the 21st seed at all.

The world number eight's exit means de Minaur is certain to be seeded in the top eight at Flushing Meadows, still ensuring the Australian does not run into a higher-ranked player until at least the quarterfinals.

But with Carlos Alcaraz still injured, de Minaur could have snatched a US Open top-four seeding and been guaranteed to avoid heavyweights such as Jannik Sinner and Alexander Zverev until at least the semifinals.

Australian qualifier Chris O'Connell plays his fourth-round match in Cincinnati later on Thursday against American sixth seed Taylor Fritz.

AAP

title: 'Have they brought value?': McIlroy fires shot at returning LIV Golf stars
text:
Masters champion Rory McIlroy believes it could be a "tough road back" for LIV Golf players who may be eyeing a return to the PGA Tour and questioned what value they would even offer the US-based circuit.

McIlroy, speaking to reporters ahead of this week's BMW Championship, needed a brief moment to reflect before answering a question on whether the possibility of players returning from LIV Golf brings value to the PGA Tour.

"I mean, I would argue, have they brought value to LIV? You know?" McIlroy said at Bellerive Country Club in St Louis, Missouri.

"I think the PGA Tour's in a really good spot."

Australia's Cameron Smith is among the LIV Golf cohort that is yet to return to the PGA Tour. (Getty Images: Jamie Squire)

LIV Golf is wrapping up its 2026 season this week near Indianapolis and said earlier this month that it had secured a lead investor that will provide a funding boost as it prepares for a future without backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

It remains unclear, however, whether major champions ⁠Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm, two of LIV Golf's biggest draws, will stay on with the rebel circuit beyond this season or seek a return to the PGA Tour.

Brooks Koepka took advantage of a limited-time Returning Member Program in early 2026 to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV Golf last December.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the five-time major winner facing a five-year forfeiture of potential equity in the PGA Tour's Player Equity Program, representing an estimated $50–85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

DeChambeau, Rahm and former British Open champion Cameron Smith were also eligible to return under the same Returning Member Program that closed on February 2 after a three-week application window.

McIlroy said he was pretty certain that any additional returning players would not be welcomed back straight away.

"If they were offered this returning member program back in February, the one that Brooks took, then, yeah, maybe. But that has sort of come and gone," he said.

"And I think it was said at the time that the deal that they might get going forward, if they do decide to come back, isn't going to be as good as the one that Brooks got. So, yeah, I would say it's going to be a tough, tough road back."

Reuters

title: Central Queensland advances bid for major defence hub
text:
A new army vehicle has defence officials very excited.

The Boxer Block II Combat Reconnaissance Vehicle has faced its most significant field test to date in central Queensland, after thousands of army personnel practised combat skills on a simulated battlefield with a live enemy, civilians and even a mock TV crew.

The Boxer Block vehicles are named after fallen soldiers. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Johnson says the vehicle is bringing the army into the digital age.

"This vehicle is a step change in capability from the previous Australian light-armoured vehicle that the public would be [familiar] with in Iraq and Afghanistan," he said.

"Its robustness, its mobility, the way it can communicate between the vehicles, as well as the ability for the enemy to really struggle to detect the vehicle … has been a significant advantage."

Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Johnson (left) and Major Scott Ferguson with the Boxer Block II. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

Sitting 80 kilometres north of Rockhampton, Shoalwater Bay Training Area has more than 450 hectares of dense bushland and sea.

It is one of the key assets within the region that a group of central Queensland politicians will be touting in Canberra next month, when they present a business case to the federal government for greater defence investment.

The Boxer Block II Combat Reconnaissance Vehicles were tested at Shoalwater Bay, as the region pushes for more defence investment. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

The business case includes a proposal to build a defence-logistics hub to repair and maintain machinery, a medical training centre to boost the number of local health professionals, and a submarine-support facility in Gladstone.

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams said it was about identifying the Defence Force's priorities and presenting solutions.

"It's a fantastic opportunity to diversify our local economy," he said.

"If we get a stronger military and defence presence in the region, it just gives us so many more options there and buffers our local workforce."

Central Queensland mayors launched the defence proposal in July. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

A core part of the proposal is more short-term accommodation, which would serve as an athlete's village for the 2032 Olympic rowing, while also hosting defence personnel and medical specialists.

Cr Williams said it would ease the region's housing shortfall.

"We have a lot of workforce [that] fly in, fly out for the mines and other development projects in the region," he said.

"If we can start to take the pressure off the existing housing market by having a dedicated area for those workers … that frees up other opportunities for those other needs that we see in our community."

Army personnel at Shoalwater Bay, acting in civilian roles. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

Defence legacy

The land for the Shoalwater Bay facility was acquired by the Commonwealth in 1965 and was used to prepare soldiers for battle in the jungles of Vietnam.

This month, it hosted 3,000 army personnel for Exercise Pozieres Run, the army's largest collective training operation of the year.

Participants were tasked with liberating a community from enemy forces while surviving in the bush on ration packs with no beds and showers.

Brigadier Jen Harris (middle) led the recent training operation. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

Brigadier Jen Harris, who commands the army's seventh brigade, said Shoalwater Bay felt like "home ground".

"This is where I can conduct and test the brigade … to the extremities of our war-fighting capability, to bring the whole team together," she said.

Defence community researcher Amy Johnson said central Queensland's "long-standing" military history meant the region was well-placed to grow its defence sector.

"We've got some really strong existing logistics and industry," Dr Johnson said.

"Things like Rocky Airport and the Port of Gladstone."

Personnel also have access to a simulation hospital at Shoalwater Bay. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

David Andrews, a senior policy adviser at the ANU's National Security College, said the project may face challenges with labour shortages and costs.

"There's a few really big defence-led infrastructure projects going on at the moment that are pulling in lots of focus," he said.

" Inevitably, workforce is a challenge as well as purely the cost of a lot of the building materials that we're getting that are caught up with the trouble in the Middle East. "

David Andrews says there are challenges to building new facilities, but the argument for readiness is compelling. (Supplied: David Andrews)

Mr Andrews said while the government's AUKUS nuclear submarines project was chewing up a lot of the defence budget, there was certainly an appetite for other projects to increase the country's national resilience.

"The National Defence Strategy has outlined the fact that we no longer have what is described as 10-year strategic warning time, which means we have to prepare for the hopefully remote prospect of conflict much, much sooner than within 10 years," he said.

"That means we have to make investments now to support that to keep Australia safe."

Exercise Pozieres Run means no showers, no beds, and living on ration packs for thousands of army personnel. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Defence said infrastructure in northern Australia was essential for Australia's capabilities.

"Defence remains committed to maximising opportunities for local industry in northern and central Queensland, with ongoing prospects for businesses in logistics, maintenance, administrative and transport support," the statement said.

Experts say Shoalwater Bay is an essential site for the ADF to train and prepare for combat. (ABC News: Jacob Gamble)

title: CLP fielding slew of amendments to VAD bill from its own backbenchers
text:
The Northern Territory government is fielding a landslide of amendments to its Rights of the Terminally Ill bill from its own backbenchers, days out from a historic conscience vote on the matter.

The bill, introduced by the Country Liberal Party (CLP) last month, would allow some terminally ill people to access voluntary assisted dying (VAD) to end their life, as is legal in all other states and territories.

But VAD advocates have criticised the bill for requiring patients to have a 12-month end-of-life prognosis and for preventing health workers from starting conversations with patients about voluntary dying.

Tanzil Rahman says there is wide-ranging recognition that the VAD bill needs some changes made to it. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Member for Fong Lim Tanzil Rahman is one of several CLP backbenchers planning to move amendments to the bill, saying there is wide-ranging recognition it should be changed.

"There are people in my own party, from other parties, from across the community, who are all rallying behind the idea that we should get the VAD bill right the first time," he said.

His amendments, released today, re-write the bill to remove the 12-month prognosis period and provide a more precise definition of someone with an "advanced" terminal illness.

They also lift the gag clause on health workers initiating conversations about VAD with eligible patients, providing they also inform them of palliative care and treatment options.

Under another of Mr Rahman's proposed amendments, relevant service providers who ethically oppose VAD will have to refer people seeking information about it to a specialist.

"What I've endeavoured to do is reflect the best practice standard across the country," Mr Rahman said.

Laurie Zio will propose the gag clause and 12-month prognosis period be removed. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

CLP Member for Fannie Bay Laurie Zio has also proposed her own amendments to the bill, which would remove the gag clause and the 12-month prognosis period.

While the government has guaranteed it has the numbers to pass the bill in its current form, Ms Zio said she was far from confident any of the proposed amendments would succeed.

NT voluntary assisted dying bill has numbers to pass The Northern Territory is set to make voluntary assisted dying legal in August. The ABC understands all 17 Country Liberal Party government members will vote in favour of the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act.

"People will come to the table and decide on the day, given it is a conscience vote," she said.

"I'm hoping people will come to the table on these two specific amendments, but there's no guarantee at all as to what will happen."

The ABC understands Member for Drysdale Clinton Howe and Member for Karama Brian O'Gallagher will also move amendments to the bill.

Pressure mounts behind-the-scenes

As a raft of proposals appear from the backbench, CLP members are facing mounting pressure from behind the scenes to amend the bill.

In early August, directors of the party's North Darwin and Trower branches wrote to Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro urging the removal of the prognosis period and gag clause.

Lia Finocchiaro has received correspondence from Labor directors urging her to make amendments to the bill. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Among the letter's signatories were former member for Sanderson and current North Darwin branch chair Daryl Manzie and former member for Jingili Rick Setter.

"Conservative legislation should not be measured by how restrictive it is, but by how effectively it balances individual liberty with appropriate protection," the letter read.

" Legislation should remove unnecessary barriers to the exercise of lawful rights, not create them. "

While most CLP members not moving amendments have remained tight-lipped about the matter, Member for Blain Matthew Kerle has come out in support of the proposals.

Politician proposes changes to NT VAD bill An NT government backbencher will move amendments to his own party's long-awaited bill to introduce voluntary assisted dying in the Territory to make it "consistent with best practice".

"If amendments are proposed that seek to remove the 12-month prognosis time limit and to remove the restrictions on doctors discussing VAD with patients, I will support those amendments," he said in a statement.

Contrastingly, Member for Goyder Andrew Mackay has said his constituents seemed to support the inclusion of the gag clause.

"Clause 16 represents an important safeguard in ensuring that the VAD process is entirely patient led and driven," he said in a statement.

"The survey results I have received indicate my community support the retention of this clause."

Moment of "maturity" on the cards

Opposition and crossbench members have voiced broad support for any amendments that will make the bill less restrictive.

"I will be supporting any amendments to make sure this bill actually reflects what the community wants," said independent member for Johnston Justine Davis.

"We didn't get this far through people giving up and saying, 'We'll just accept what's there,'" she said.

Acting Leader of the Opposition Ed Smelt said Territory Labor has their own amendments but are aligned in principle with Mr Rahman's proposal.

Ed Smelt says Territory Labor's amendments are aligned with those proposed by Mr Rahman's. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Our view has always been that we would not stand in the way of Territorians having access to voluntary assisted dying," he said.

He said Labor would be looking at the gag clause, the prognosis timeframe and the role of faith-based centres in providing information to those interested.

"We'll have a look at the final detail and we'll see how that aligns with our amendments, but I do stress this is a conscience vote for Labor members as well," he said.

Labor member for Gwoja Chansey Paech has previously stated he will abstain from a vote around VAD.

Chansey Paech will abstain from the VAD vote. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Any amendments to the bill will require the support of at least five more CLP members or Speaker of the House Robyn Lambley should the remaining Labor MLAs along with Ms Davis, Mr Rahman, Ms Zio and Ms Kerle support the same amendment.

Mr Rahman, whose amendments were informed by his work on the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee report into VAD last year, said he remained hopeful.

"It's not insignificant that three CLP members, a Labor member and a Green all unanimously agreed on the recommendations of that report, and that's not something that happens in the Territory parliament very often," he said.

"I now hope desperately that our parliament will demonstrate maturity whilst using a conscience vote to work together."

title: Socceroos star Circati seals $33m transfer move to Portuguese giants
text:
Young Socceroo Alessandro Circati has become the latest Australian international to be snapped up in a money-spinning European transfer, as he hails his move from Parma to Benfica as a "privilege".

Following Lucas Herrington's move from the MLS to become Australia's only Premier League player at Hull City, and Nestory Irankunda joining Benfica's great rivals Sporting from Watford, Circati has been signed by the Portuguese giants for a reported 20 million euros ($33 million).

With Nishan Velupillay's move from Melbourne Victory to third-tier German club FC Ingolstadt 04 also completed on Wednesday, World Cup Socceroos are clearly the flavour of the month, with other reports linking top clubs with Norwich striker Mohamed Toure.

Circati's move from the Italian top-flight Serie A to Portugal's Primeira Liga has been in the pipeline for a while, with the 22-year-old having signed a five-year contract through to 2031 with the Lisbon-based double European champions.

"To all the Benfiquistas, yeah, I can't wait to play in front of you all, and win as many titles as we can. It's a huge honour. It's a privilege. I'm over the moon, couldn't be happier," Circati said in a message to the fans on the club's website.

"I think it's a reward for many years of hard work. I'm so happy to be here, and I can't wait to play for Benfica."

The Italian-born Circati will play at the world-famous Estadio da Luz — the Stadium of Light — and sounded just a little awe-struck as he added: "I can't wait. I've just had a look at it now. It's amazing, and I'm very, very excited to play."

Socceroos forward Nishan Velupillay (right) is also moving to a new club, joining Germany's FC Ingolstadt 04. (Reuters: Albert Gea)

Asked about adapting quickly to his move, he added: "I think I'm very adaptable. I think you can play me in either role of the centre-back, in a back-four or a back-three.

"I'm sure it's going to take a bit of time to adapt, but I'll try and make it as fast as possible with the help of my teammates and staff. But I'm sure I'll fit in just fine."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The lad who came through the ranks at Perth Glory and, after completing a trial with Parma in 2021, returned to his Italian roots to join them, has made swift and impressive progress in Serie A, last year being a stand-out for the northern club as they finished 12th.

Circati also played in all four of the Socceroos' World Cup matches, with 17 international appearances now under his belt and one goal to his name.

Parma paid tribute to his time at the club in a statement, saying: "Alessandro made a total of 96 appearances for Parma, including 37 in Serie A, scoring two goals and playing a key role not only in the club's 2023/24 Serie B title triumph but also in securing survival over the following two seasons.

"President Kyle J. Krause, CEO Federico Cherubini and the entire Parma Calcio family would like to sincerely thank Alessandro and wish him every success in the next chapter of his career."

AAP

title: Industry condemns labour hire company that misled inspectors on farm
text:
The Queensland Strawberry Growers Association president has condemned the operators of a former labour hire provider for deliberately falsifying documents and breaching workplace laws.

On August 13, the Federal Circuit and Family Court ordered Korserv Pty Ltd to pay $150,240 and fined its former manager, Janghwan Choi, $30,048.

The Fair Work Ombudsman is taking action to protect workers. (Supplied: Fair Work Ombudsman)

The court heard both admitted to providing false and misleading documents to a Fair Work inspector on a Glass House Mountains farm in December 2023 and January 2024.

Korserv, which is no longer operating, was being audited for compliance with pay rates for 14 farm workers, including at least three visa holders.

The Fair Work audit took place on a Glass House Mountains farm in 2023. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The falsified documents included pay slips, payment records purportedly from Korserv's bank account that were never made, superannuation records, and piecework agreements containing false signatures.

The court was told that Korserv had subcontracted two other companies, which were responsible for paying the workers at the farm, and had sent money to those subcontractors.

Fair Work was undertaking an audit on a Glass House Mountains strawberry farm. (Supplied: Fair Work Ombudsman)

Court judgment

In his judgment, Judge Gregory Egan described the "production of the false and misleading documents" as "egregious flouting" of workplace laws.

"The intention on the part of the respondents was to mislead the inspector," he said.

"Penalties ought to be imposed which will generally deter any future conduct of a similar nature by others."

Adrian Schultz says the behaviour is "very disappointing". (ABC Rural: Melanie Groves)

Queensland Strawberry Growers president Adrian Schultz welcomed the fines, but said the punishment should have been harsher.

"It's a very small percentage of people who are taking advantage of these workers and I don't think the penalty is enough," Mr Schultz said.

Korserv Pty Ltd had been hired to provide labour services to the farm. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The judgment states Korserv was engaged by Twin Creek Junction Pty Ltd to provide labour hire services, but it did not suggest any wrongdoing on the farm's part.

The strawberry business entered voluntary administration last year.

Its fields remain barren, home to rusting equipment, weeds and perishing rows of plastic.

The court heard Korserv subcontracted two other companies who were responsible for paying farm workers. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) Anna Booth said her office was prioritising trying to "rid the agriculture sector of this sort of behaviour".

"The conduct in this case was a blatant breach of workplace laws," Ms Booth said.

"We treat breaches of workplace laws involving visa-holder workers particularly seriously because they can be vulnerable, often unaware of their rights, heavily reliant on their employers or reluctant to complain."

Anna Booth says she is focused on compliance in the agriculture sector. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Mr Schultz encouraged concerned workers to contact the ombudsman. Complaints can be made anonymously, with language-translation services provided.

"We don't have a business if these people don't come and work and so it's very disappointing when these things happen," he said.

The farm that employed the labour hire company has since ceased operation. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The FWO website can be searched to check if labour hire contractors are registered and if action has been taken against them.

"A farmer would have rocks in his head to employ a labour hire contractor … without checking them out first," Mr Schultz said.

Korserv Pty Ltd and Mr Choi were given 30 days to pay the fines.

In its judgment, the court accepted "a level of contrition and co-operation has been demonstrated on the part of the second respondent", Mr Choi.

title: Call to bail out Australia's last remaining nickel smelter
text:
A WA Liberal MP says Australia's only nickel smelter should be next in line for a government bailout as mining giant BHP mulls its future.

The company's Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter was mothballed in 2024 after 51 years of operations.

Rick Wilson, whose federal electorate of O'Connor includes Kalgoorlie-Boulder, is pushing for the same sort of Commonwealth support for the smelter that has been provided for metal smelters elsewhere.

In the past year, the federal government has committed a combined $1.67 billion to ensure four smelters on the east coast stay open — including a $2.5 billion deal announced last week to secure the future of Tomago Aluminium.

The Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter was officially opened by former prime minister Gough Whitlam in 1973. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Nickel was added to the government's Critical Minerals List in February 2024.

"Are jobs in the Hunter Valley worth more than in the Goldfields?" Mr Wilson said in a statement to the ABC.

"No support has been offered for the nickel industry which is also classified as a strategically important mineral.

Neil Thomson, Rick Wilson, Matt Canavan and Goldfields mining industry stalwart Graham McGarry at the smelter in December. (Supplied: Facebook/Rick Wilson)

"The bigger picture is that the safeguard mechanism is destroying the viability of our heavy industries and forcing the taxpayer to subsidise industries which the government's policy have made unviable."

Taxpayer bailouts adding up

Last year, the federal opposition unsuccessfully lobbied for a Senate inquiry into Australia's metals manufacturing industry, claiming 10 smelters and refineries across Australia were in danger of closing due to high energy prices.

Last week's Tomago deal follows a string of similar bailouts the Albanese government has offered to struggling heavy industries, including Glencore's Mount Isa copper smelter and the Nyrstar smelters in Tasmania and South Australia.

The ABC asked WA-based Resources Minister Madeleine King if the federal government was working on a potential funding package to save the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter and Nickel West.

The entrance to the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter is decorated with hats and ID tags of workers who signed off for the last time in late 2024. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

In response, the ABC received a statement from the office of Industry Minister Tim Ayres, who described nickel as "an important critical mineral for Australia" with a "key role in our industrial future".

"The Commonwealth continues to work productively and collaboratively with state governments and facility owners," the statement read.

Bailouts questioned

But City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder mayor Glenn Wilson, who also chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance, said government bailouts were "sugar hits" to businesses without long-term planning to support affected communities.

"The alliance understands obviously it's important to have these facilities up and available for our communities," he said.

Glenn Wilson chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance, which comprises six local governments across the country, including the historic mining centres of Mount Isa and Broken Hill. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"But at the same time, government handouts are not the way of the future.

"Does that mean that when those government handouts finish we are just prolonging the inevitable, or are we trying to support our communities in the longer term?"

The Murrin Murrin nickel-cobalt mine in WA's northern Goldfields was officially opened in July 1999. (Supplied: Glencore/Facebook)

The future is not looking especially bright for WA's two remaining nickel mines, Glencore's Murrin Murrin mine and IGO's Nova nickel-copper mine.

Nova is set to close by the end of the year and be converted into a lithium processing facility.

Meanwhile, Glencore announced to the London Stock Exchange on August 5 it had written down the value of Murrin Murrin by $US457 million to zero in the current market.

BHP deadline approaching

The dire situation for WA's once-booming nickel industry comes six months before BHP is due to make a call on the future of its Nickel West division.

Only a tiny fraction of workers stayed on at the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter when it was placed into care and maintenance. (Supplied: BHP)

Only a handful of the 3,500-strong workforce stayed on at Nickel West when the smelter was mothballed.

The company declined taxpayer support in 2024 when it announced its "temporary suspension" and committed to reviewing its nickel business by February 2027.

"As part of this review, BHP is assessing the potential divestment of the Western Australia nickel assets," the company's annual report stated on Tuesday after posting a $US9.8 billion profit for the 2025-26 financial year.

"Any decision to divest will be subject to an assessment against other options, including continuing temporary suspension, restart or closure."

title: FIFA vice-president withdraws support for Infantino after 'final straw'
text:
More national football federations and FIFA officials have withdrawn their support for the football body's president, Gianni Infantino, after the exit of chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, which one FIFA vice-president described as the "final straw".

FIFA said on Tuesday (AEST) that Lamour had left the organisation. It came weeks after he publicly criticised Mr Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other tournaments.

His exit prompted Hungary's Sandor Csanyi — one of eight FIFA vice-presidents and a member of the FIFA Council — to withdraw his support for the embattled Mr Infantino, who is under pressure from three confederations to resign.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"The final straw was the unexpected dismissal of Kevin Lamour," Mr Csanyi wrote in a letter to Infantino, seen by Reuters.

"Kevin performed his duties to a high professional and ethical standard and, as a highly competent executive, made a significant contribution to the transparent operation of the organisation.

"The fact that his dismissal was prompted by his criticism of the above-mentioned initiative — an initiative that you yourself ultimately acknowledged to have been misguided — points to serious shortcomings in professional judgement, ethical standards and leadership."

FIFA did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr Lamour had said staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Other FIFA vice-presidents who have attacked Mr Infantino's conduct are UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa, and CONCACAF president Vittorio Montagliani.

'Extremely worrying'

Dejan Savicevic has labelled recent developments at FIFA under Infantino's tenure "extremely worrying". (Getty Images: Gualter Fatia)

Montenegro's Dejan Savicevic, a FIFA Council member since 2017 and president of the country's football association, said they had also withdrawn their earlier letter of support for Mr Infantino's candidacy.

Mr Infantino is up for re-election in March and is seeking a fourth term until 2031.

Mr Savicevic wrote a letter to FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström outlining his concerns.

"The recent developments within FIFA are extremely worrying and have shown a serious lack of communication and transparency not only to the member associations … but also to the internal members, FIFA Council included, and structures which should hold the foundations of FIFA," he wrote.

"The proposals put forward exposed concerning vulnerabilities regarding governance, not only at the political level but also within the FIFA administration.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The Football Association of Montenegro agrees with the opinion of other European national associations and UEFA and demands a thorough review of the actions of the FIFA leadership," he added.

Israel has also withdrawn its support for Mr Infantino's re-election, according to The Guardian, with the decision being taken unanimously after a meeting of the IFA's board.

Football Association of Wales (FAW) chief executive Noel Mooney told the BBC that Mr Infantino should resign after his doomed proposal to "sell off the crown jewels" to private equity investors.

Earlier this month, Wales became the first national federation to withdraw its support for Mr Infantino formally.

Despite the opposition of the three confederations, African confederation CAF and South America's CONMEBOL are currently on Mr Infantino's side.

CAF president Patrice Motsepe, who is also a FIFA vice-president, warned any attempt to remove him should be decided democratically by FIFA's 211-member associations at next year's elections, rather than through other means.

A CAF spokesperson said Mr Motsepe had nothing further to add after Mr Lamour's exit.

Reuters

title: Prince Harry, Meghan and family to move back to UK, the ABC understands
text:
Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are planning to move back to the UK this month, the ABC understands.

Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and his wife intend to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence outside London, the BBC reported.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, are also expected to start at a British school in September.

British media first reported the news, but spokespeople for ⁠Harry and Meghan had no immediate ‌comment. However, a source close to the couple confirmed the report's accuracy.

King Charles was told of the move on Sunday, local time, and it is understood he welcomed the move.

Earlier in July, the family met with King Charles in what was widely seen as a thawing of frosty relations.

King hosts Harry and family at private residence The royal couple hosted the duke and duchess and their children Archie and Lilibet at a country retreat.

It was the first time in four years that the couple's seven-year-old son and five-year-old daughter had visited the UK, with Buckingham Palace describing the meeting as a "private family occasion".

Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since 2022, when they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II.

But even the run-up to the July trip was rocked by setbacks, with media outlets quoting sources close to Harry as saying the prince would be staying at Buckingham Palace in London — only for the palace to deny it.

The palace said Harry had not accepted the invitation to stay at the official residence of the British sovereign sufficiently far in advance.

The three men of the royal family have had frosty relations since 2020. (Reuters: Philippe Huguen)

It has been six years since Harry and Meghan stepped down from their royal duties.

There are no public plans for either to resume those roles.

Buckingham Palace revealed in February 2024 that King Charles was undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer.

He is still receiving treatment but said last December an early diagnosis and effective intervention meant this could be scaled back.

The Harry and Meghan news coincides with a release from Queen Camilla, who spoke publicly for the first time about how hard it was to keep the king's cancer diagnosis private at first.

Harry wants protection. The women who could help are the ones he's lost Prince Harry may be testing the thread of unconditional love that is supposed to connect a parent and child. But in royal life, that thread is stitched into a complicated tapestry, frayed by protocol, duty and terms set by the king.

Harry married Meghan Markle in a dazzling ceremony at Windsor Castle in 2018, and it was hoped his union with the former actress, whose mother is Black, would reinvigorate the historic institution.

But it was not long before cracks in their relationship with the rest of the royal family began to emerge.

After stepping away from royal duties, they moved to the wealthy seaside enclave of Montecito near Santa Barbara, California, with media reports putting the 2020 purchase price of their 16-bedroom home at $ US14.7 million ($20.6m).

In the following years, Harry, now 41, and Meghan, 45, repeatedly criticised the royal family and the monarchy in TV interviews, a Netflix documentary series and most notably in Harry's memoir Spare.

Harry has long blamed the media for the death of his mother, Princess Diana, who was killed in a Paris car crash in 1997 while trying to shake off the paparazzi.

While Harry and the king's relationship may have improved, he is still barely on speaking terms with his brother, Prince William.

ABC/Wires

title: Olympic questions 'off limits' ahead of Rockhampton schools' rowing regatta
text:
Rowing Queensland has imposed new media restrictions on athletes, coaches and rowing representatives ahead of an upcoming state schools regatta at the proposed Brisbane 2032 rowing venue.

Next month's Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will bring more than 800 school-aged rowers from across Queensland to Rockhampton for three days of racing on the Fitzroy River, the controversial venue selected to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Olympics and Paralympics.

It will be the first state-level rowing event held at the venue in five years, placing a renewed spotlight on the Fitzroy River's suitability for major competition.

Rockhampton school rowers training on the Fitzroy River. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

But in a significant development, the ABC understands local rowing representatives preparing for the championships were told they could not discuss or promote the Olympics in media interviews.

Rowing Queensland has confirmed it introduced a stricter media accreditation process for the event amid heightened media interest and safeguarding concerns around school-aged rowers.

Chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin said she appreciated the increased interest in rowing in Rockhampton given its link to Brisbane 2032, but the schools' regatta should not be viewed as a test or demonstration event for the Olympics.

Tim Mander (far left) and David Crisafulli (centre) meet school rowers on the Fitzroy River, the proposed venue for rowing at the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

"At the request of the local rowing club, Rowing Queensland has introduced a media accreditation process for the championship," Ms O'Loughlin said.

" Our priority is to provide an environment where school-aged athletes can train and compete safely, without additional media pressure or disruption. "

She said locals were free to discuss the Olympics and events coming to Rockhampton but stressed the upcoming regatta was a school event being held on infrastructure appropriate for school sport.

The Queensland government has repeatedly defended the Fitzroy River as a suitable venue for the 2032 Games, dismissing concerns about the natural river course, flooding, crocodiles, infrastructure and racing conditions.

Jarrod Bleijie says the rowing will happen on the Fitzroy River for the 2032 Games. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Speaking in Toowoomba on Thursday morning, Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said he was disappointed there were restrictions on "people talking positively about rowing on the mighty Fitzroy River".

"People should be able to talk openly about the benefits of regional Queensland, the benefits of rowing on the mighty Fitzroy River and how great it's going to be in 2032," he said.

" Secondly, I'd say this: I might even go now. I might go to the state championships because I'd love to see some of these organisations try and gag me from speaking to the media, particularly about how great rowing at the 2032 Games is going to be on the mighty Fitzroy River. "

Members of the CQ32 Rowing Legacy Advisory Committee, which is championing the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing and canoeing at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The Olympic proposal

The proposal to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River was first championed by a Central Queensland advocacy group which included Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan.

"The Rockhampton rowing course is at the centre of everything with an airport, highway and a CBD within minutes," Senator Canavan said at the time.

"It just all stacks up. I think the Games should deliver for all of Queensland."

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart also wrote to Queensland's deputy premier advocating for Olympic rowing and canoeing to be held in Rockhampton before the venue was selected.

Australian rowers have previously used the Fitzroy River as a training venue before the Olympics. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland supports the Queensland government in hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the state but says the proposed Rockhampton venue remains subject to the technical and venue planning processes associated with hosting an Olympic event.

Ms O'Loughlin said the existing Rockhampton course and infrastructure were appropriate for a school-level competition but were not representative of what would be required for a national, international or Olympic rowing event.

"The rowing community awaits the release of information on the Olympic venue location and infrastructure, which has yet to be published by the Queensland government," she said.

A crocodile warning sign at the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Tobias Jurss-Lewis)

Scrutiny of venue

Concerns have nevertheless been raised by rowing bodies and elite Australian rowers about fairness, tidal currents and the suitability of a natural river course, including issues around flooding and crocodile management, with some advocating for dedicated facilities in south-east Queensland or interstate.

Rowing Australia said the technical assessment of the Rockhampton venue was a matter for the relevant authorities, including World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee.

It said it would continue to support key stakeholders involved in planning for Brisbane 2032.

An electronic billboard in Rockhampton has been up for several months, alternating between designs promoting the Olympics for central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Asked where Rowing Queensland believed Olympic rowing should be held, Ms O'Loughlin said the organisation was not involved in the venue-selection process.

"Rowing Queensland's position is that Olympic rowing should be held in Queensland at a venue that meets the technical requirements for Olympic competition and receives the necessary approval through the Olympic venue-assessment process," she said.

"Rowing Queensland awaits the outcomes of the relevant technical review, including the assessment by World Rowing."

Australian rowers Jess Morrison and Annabelle McIntyre competing at the 2024 Paris Olympics. (AAP via Photosport: Iain McGregor)

'Games for Queensland'

In March, the state's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority progressed its feasibility assessment for the Rockhampton Flatwater Facility to evaluate two preferred layouts, moving the high-stakes 2032 Games venue into its next detailed planning phase.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the latest progress ensured the Rockhampton community and competitors could have confidence in the Fitzroy.

Hundreds of athletes will compete in state championship events from year 9 through to year 12 next month. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

"The Crisafulli government promised a Games and generational legacy for all Queenslanders, including rowing and canoeing in Rocky," Mr Bleijie said.

"We're working well with the rowing and canoeing international federations, as well as the IOC and our Games delivery partners to deliver an incredible venue and competition in 2032, and a long-lasting legacy for Rockhampton."

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will be held on the Fitzroy River from September 19 to 21, marking the pinnacle event and conclusion of the 2026 Queensland school rowing season.

title: Longmire reveals 'deep sadness' over Swans' links to police probe
text:
Sydney's last premiership coach says there is a deep sense of sadness at five banned Swans players being linked to allegations of sexual assault.

John Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach, says the suspensions of five players are "flattening" for all involved.

Swans Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon are linked to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel on Monday morning.

'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad detectives are expected to soon arrive in Sydney to further their investigations.

The players are yet to be formally interviewed or charged, and it is not suggested that any of them are being accused of sexual assault.

The bans instead related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, for which they have apologised.

Longmire, who is currently the club's executive director of club performance, said the on-field ramifications of banning the players were not a priority for the Swans hierarchy.

"It was just incredible deep sadness … and that is probably where we're still sitting," he told Fox Footy on Wednesday night.

Longmire was the coach when Sydney won its most recent AFL premiership in 2012. (AAP: Joe Castro)

"Football aspirations weren't part of the discussions, they were very much in the background.

"At the forefront were other people issues — as they should have been.

"The people issues are the things that really led the discussions over the last few days … the premiership discussions were at the very back-end of anything that was talked about."

The second-placed Swans, with one home-and-away game remaining, are assured of hosting two finals as they seek to win the club's first premiership since under Longmire in 2012.

"It's flattening for a lot of people," he said.

John Longmire with Isaac Heeney after the 2024 preliminary final. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

"It's a challenge for everybody to be able to get through and be able to put one foot in front of the other and get things right.

"We feel for everybody."

Longmire was Sydney's head coach from 2011 to 2024 after being an assistant from 2002.

"The culture of the footy club has taken a big hit, and it will take time for everyone to rebuild the trust in the football club," he said.

"You go from shock and disappointment, maybe a bit of anger in that. You get a bit of those emotions.

"And you also care about people, try and get that balance right, and it's very tricky."

The five players on Wednesday evening apologised in a joint statement issued by the Swans.

"We are deeply sorry to everyone involved," they said. "We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club.

"We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved."

Meanwhile, Readings Books and Gleebooks have confirmed they have removed Heeney's children's book series, Little Isaac Footy Fever, for purchase, after Allen & Unwin also removed promotions for the books from their Instagram grid.

Booktopia said they will continue to stock the book but will assess the situation.

"We're working closely with the publisher regarding their plans and will continue to assess the situation," a statement provided to the ABC said.

"Our mandate is to provide a service and selection of books in the best interest of our customers. We appreciate the sensitivity and will carefully consider any decision, together with the publisher, in due course."

ABC/AAP

title: Meet the FIFO workers keeping mining towns dancing all night
text:
Of the estimated 60,000 fly-in-fly-out workers in Western Australia, Benny Gee is one of a few that have nothing to do with the resources industry.

Every two months, Benny flies 1,550 kilometres north of Perth to perform at a regional nightclub in the iron ore mining hub of Karratha.

"I'd never heard of FIFO DJing until they came up and approached me," he said.

" Obviously everyone around me is FIFO doing mining jobs, and there's just me flying up and playing music. "

Benny, who is a sales representative, usually flies out on a Friday afternoon to play two nights, returning on a Sunday.

"It is a big shift, you start at 10pm and sometimes you work until 4:30 or 5am ... it's sort of preparing me for what I want to do which is tour the world with my music," he said.

DJ Benny Gee says the FIFO DJ lifestyle is special. (Supplied: DJ Benny Gee/ Good Karma Music)

Now four years into the gig, he said it has been a good opportunity to spread his music to new audiences.

"[Regional crowds] go a little bit more nuts than the city people and it's awesome," he said.

"It's just a different energy."

The DJs play shows on Friday and Saturday nights. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

'Like a holiday'

Alex Kozza, another FIFO DJ, flies to northern WA every two to three weeks and said it was like a going on a holiday.

DJ Kozza says he has developed strong relationships with the community after years of performing. (Supplied: DJ Kozza)

"I love the weather up there ... it's like a little vacation, I get to change it up from weekly DJing in Perth," the 21-year-old said.

He said many people were surprised by his job.

"People are honestly shocked — when people think of DJ they either think of club DJs in Perth or they think of the massive people playing huge festivals internationally.

" People don't realise that, at my level, people get flown across the country just to play these regional clubs. "

Karratha's night scene in full flight on a Saturday. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Three years into playing at Karratha, Alex said he has developed strong friendships.

"Every time I go up there now they will pick me up from the airport, or we will play golf," he said.

Not for everyone

Booking agent John Fraser manages about 10 FIFO DJs who work at regional clubs in various remote locations, including Broome and Port Hedland.

Mr Fraser said he started booking multiple DJs in Karratha shortly after COVID.

"Before they [venues] were just booking the same DJ from Perth who was going up every weekend back and forth and it got to a point where the owner of the club wanted just a bit more variety," he said.

"That's why we've got a group of DJs, not just one or two DJs."

DJs are flown to remote parts of Australia to give audiences a variety of entertainment. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

He said the lifestyle was not for everybody.

"I think it's a gig for a young person, while they're still single or don't have families," he said.

" It takes a certain kind of DJ to want to do it, and those that do really love it. "

While some regional pubs and clubs pubs book local talent, he said some specific venues continue to prefer to fly in DJs.

"There is definitely now some good talent in Karratha, but I guess it comes down to each venue and what they decide to do."

title: Backpackers crucial to business, say farmers as visa approvals pause
text:
Farmers fear a federal government pause on working holiday visa approvals will rob them of an essential workforce and put Australia's food security at risk.

Australia's Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program started in 1975 and is regarded as mutually beneficial for farmers, rural communities and overseas backpackers who get to travel the country and work along the way.

Richard Shannon says fewer backpackers would put the country's food security at risk. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

The National Farmers Federation (NFF) estimates that backpackers make up about half of Australia's peak-harvest casual workforce and says any cuts are alarming.

"[Backpackers] are essential to our industry and the food security of the nation," horticulture spokesman Richard Shannon said.

'Rural people will suffer'

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed on Sunday that WHM visas were being processed "more slowly than they were previously".

The government website for the WHM visas shows applications from 24 countries have been paused.

The pause on visa approvals comes amid furious debate about the future of Australia's migration policy.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has not guaranteed backpackers will be exempt from the Coalition's planned cuts to migration.

But Nationals leader Matt Canavan has previously promised his party would not allow any changes, arguing working holiday-makers are crucial for rural communities.

Backpackers in times of crisis

Australian charity BlazeAid organises volunteers to clean up and rebuild farms and fences after fires, floods and cyclones.

Backpackers make up a large proportion of the organisation's helpers.

"I just worry that if this slowdown occurs, then our Australian society and particularly rural people will suffer," BlazeAid chief executive Melissa Jones said.

Melissa Jones (left, with her parents Kevin and Rhonda Butler) is worried about disaster recovery and the agriculture workforce. (Supplied: Melissa Jones)

"At our base camp in Euroa [in Victoria] at the moment, where we're working after the Longwood fires, [and] 75 per cent of those in camp are backpackers."

Ms Jones said the benefit of having working holiday makers went "well beyond the fences that we rebuild."

"They spend money in the local shops, they stay in the local communities, they create connections with people in towns," she said.

"They're not buying our houses, they're not taking the space that we need.

"They're actually very beneficial to our country, and it should stay that way."

South Australian potato grower Terry Buckley said backpackers were also crucial to his business.

"We usually have some backpackers when we're cutting our seed potatoes for planting and … when we're harvesting in autumn."

Terry Buckley says that without backpackers, he would have to buy expensive machinery. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

Mr Buckley said, without them, he would have to buy more machinery.

"There's a lot of machinery that's $1 million a piece now, so that's all got to be recouped somehow," he said.

Pacific workers 'not a substitute'

When confirming the slowing of approvals, Mr Burke argued the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme was the "principal visa for the agriculture industry."

But Mr Shannon said there was plenty of work for both PALM workers and backpackers.

"They are not substitutes. They fill different roles and purposes, both in a very practical sense on farm but in terms of the sort of labour need they meet," he said.

Australia's largest grower of Kensington Pride and R2E2 mangoes, Manbulloo in the Northern Territory, uses PALM workers as well as backpackers.

"A base level of seasonal workers comes from the Pacific, but if we need additional people in the team, we employ backpackers," managing director Marie Piccone said.

Marie Piccone says she needs PALM workers and backpackers to pick mangoes. (Supplied: Businesswomen Hall of Fame)

She said the PALM scheme was more expensive and took longer.

"It's about 10 times the administration and a significantly more costly scheme than just employing Australians under the same rates and conditions, or employing backpackers," Ms Piccone said.

"We need to have our workforce to get our mango crop off because that's the one time of the year where we get our income."

'Cost price squeeze'

Farming groups, including BlazeAid, have written to Mr Burke urging him to consider the importance of backpackers.

"I think that the ministers and the federal government have to understand that horticulture is in a cost price squeeze," Ms Piccone said.

The NFF's Richard Shannon said the group would take "every step possible" to ensure the government considered the risk to food security.

"And the upward pressure likely to come on the cost of fresh produce in supermarket aisles," he said.

The government has been contacted for comment.

title: Cumberland mental health patients abscond 14 times since deaths
text:
Mental health patients at Cumberland Hospital have absconded more than a dozen times since February, when two patient escapes were linked to the deaths of three people.

The government ordered an urgent security review following the February incidents, with New South Wales Premier Chris Minns declaring something had "gone badly wrong".

However, on Wednesday, a senior NSW Health official told a budget estimates hearing that at least 14 further absconding incidents had occurred at Cumberland Hospital in Sydney's west since then.

Reading from a list, the executive director of the mental health branch, Brendan Flynn, indicated there were four "type 1" cases recorded in March, three in April, two in both May and June, and another three in July.

"[Type] 1 is when someone leaves a facility. For example … getting out an air lock, or jumping over the roof, or whatever it may be," Dr Flynn said.

"And type 2 is [absconding] on escorted leave with health staff."

However, Dr Flynn said the figures equated to 0.5 absconding cases per 1,000 bed days.

"I know the rate is of no help to individuals who've been harmed," he said.

" But … it does give us a degree of confidence, in the sense that the rate is actually less than what we see elsewhere. "

Brendan Flynn says the figures equate to 0.5 absconding cases per 1,000 bed days. (ABC News)

Late on Wednesday, Dr Flynn told the hearing that another branch of the health department had "slightly different figures, which are actually lower", regarding absconding rates at Cumberland.

"They're not that different, but they're not exact," he said.

He committed to providing those figures to parliament at a later date.

Shadow Mental Health Minister Sarah Mitchell said it was "alarming" patients were still absconding from Cumberland regularly.

"It doesn't appear, based on the data we were given … that the problem is getting any better," she said.

Government will not release report

Two women died in the two-car crash at Camden earlier this year. (ABC News )

In February, the government asked the Cabinet Office to prepare a report on the escapes of two patients from Cumberland Hospital, who allegedly caused the deaths of three people.

On February 14, a 31-year-old patient allegedly caused a car crash that killed two women in Camden, having absconded six days earlier.

Then on February 17, another patient who had absconded from the mental health facility allegedly stabbed three people in Merrylands, killing one and critically injuring two others.

Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson told the hearing she was "not in a position" to release the report because its contents would be the subject of criminal proceedings.

"I would say, there was nothing in those findings that pointed to serious or significant failings," she said.

"Obviously the system didn't work well, but … we were able to act on those recommendations."

One man escaped Camden Hospital days before allegedly killing one person and critically injuring two others. (Supplied: NSW Police Force)

Ms Mitchell said Ms Jackson failed to provide answers to important questions.

"Where were the gaps in the system?" she said.

"And how did those two individuals find themselves in a position where they were able to abscond and allegedly go on to commit those horrific crimes?"

Tree branches, downpipes removed to prevent escapes

The minister did provide some details of a separate review, aimed at preventing future escapes from Cumberland Hospital.

In line with its recommendations, loose furniture was removed and replaced with items that could be bolted to the ground, she said.

Some tree branches had also been pruned and downpipes had been removed to "prevent people climbing out" onto the roof.

Rose Jackson says changes have been made to prevent future escapes. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Ms Jackson said staff leave practices had been reviewed and a risk assessment had been completed, resulting in the appointment of more security guards.

"We now have six security officers on the day shift and five security officers on night shift, including a senior security officer on each shift," she said.

Ms Mitchell said the government's reviews should have resulted in a major reduction in absconding incidents, but they had not.

"We've had two horrific incidents this year," she said.

"If that's not enough to see real change and those numbers decrease dramatically, then what is?"

Manhattan Gold Corporation has kicked off its maiden drilling campaign in Canada with a bang, delivering a spectacular intercept of 41.15 metres at 4.66 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 83.82m downhole at its Hook Lake project in Nunavut. The result from the Jaws gold target included a blistering high-grade core of 7.62m grading an impressive 18.67g/t gold from 85.34m, with two individual 1.52-metre samples returning eye watering grades as high as 41g/t and 33.4g/t gold. A reverse circulation drill rig at the Jaws prospect targeting historic gold mineralisation at Manhattan Gold Corporation’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut, Canada. The discovery comes at a time when the gold price is trading significantly higher, now above A$6300, highlighting the potential of Canada’s underexplored greenstone belts. Nunavut is proving to be a hive of activity with major players such as B2Gold advancing large-scale exploration in the region. It is also home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast, one of Canada’s largest gold mines. Manhattan’s standout drillhole represents a hefty upgrade on the nearest historic hole from the late 1980’s, which returned 22m at 2.41g/t gold. The company says its new intercept is both significantly thicker and carries a much higher grade, confirming the presence of high-grade shoots within a broader mineralised envelope.

Advertisement

‘Jaws is rapidly emerging as the high-grade gold cornerstone of a much larger,district-scale Hook Lake opportunity.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard Adding to the intrigue, the hole ended in mineralisation with a 1.52 metre hit at 0.31g/t gold from 199.64m, suggesting the system potentially remains open at depth. Manhattan Gold technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said: “These are exceptional first results for Manhattan. An intercept of 41.15m at 4.66g/t gold, including 7.62m at 18.67g/t, materially elevates the scale and grade potential of the Jaws system. The result is materially wider and higher grade than the nearest historic intercept and confirms that Jaws hosts very high-grade shoots within a broad mineralised envelope.” Other assays from the first four holes of the campaign also delivered encouraging results. One hole confirmed a broad mineralised system with a 79.25-metre intercept grading 0.78g/t gold from a shallow 38.10m. Within that zone, a higher-grade slice returned 9.14m at 2.54g/t gold. Additionally, another hole landed 9.15m at 1.99g/t gold from 153.92m, with a further hole hitting 9.15m at 1.73g/t gold from 35.05m.

Advertisement

Notably, the company says the drilling has materially improved its geological model for Jaws. The new data indicatethe main shear zone lies 20m to 30m northwest of the position inferred from historical records, providing a stronger basis to target what it interprets as high-grade plunging shoots. The Jaws target already hosts a non-JORC foreign estimate of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces, defined by drilling in the late 1980’s. Manhattan’s maiden reverse circulation drilling program at its 665-square-kilometre Hook Lake project has now surpassed 3000m across 13 drillholes, with a pipeline of assays still pending. Beyond Jaws, the Hook Lake project has a grab-bag of 12 other compelling targets. These include the never-drilled Vanquish, Quantum and Lotus prospects, which have returned surface gold samples of 20g/t, 16.75g/t and 8.01g/t respectively. With work at Jaws delivering immediate success, the company has already moved the drill rig to its next target, the high-grade Spectre copper-zinc prospect. Spectre is a volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) target with compelling historic drill results, including 10.51m at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.70 per cent zinc, 95.67g/t silver and 1.04g/t gold. In addition to the drilling, a regional till sampling program is set to fire up shortly to evaluate extensions and other targets within the Omega banded iron formation. An airborne magnetic survey is also underway to refine the geological model across the district-scale project.

With a cracking first-up drill hit significantly enhancing the grade and scale at Jaws, a newly refined geological model to chase more high-grade shoots and the drill rods already spinning at a high-grade VMS target, Manhattan appears to be just getting warmed up in the Canadian north.
