When Lucas Herrington was linked to Barcelona during the World Cup, I’m sure there were plenty of Australian fans who were excited about the prospect of seeing one of our own in that famous shirt. Instead, he’s ended up at Hull City. Loading That would be a pretty substantial downgrade if you were planning a holiday. But for a young footballer, I’m not so sure it is a downgrade at all. Only time will tell, but I think Herrington may have made exactly the right move for his career at exactly the right time.

Advertisement

For some players, the prestige and/or location of a club is a big factor in their decision when it comes to transfers. When I was playing, it was always about the football for me: what league does the club play in, what is their plan and where do I fit into it? I learnt from experience. After I left Germany, where I had limited opportunities, I decided I would never move to another club again without first speaking to the manager. Do they believe in me? Do they actually want me? How much will I play? I needed to hear it from them, in their words. Lucas Herrington will play for Hull City in the Premier League. Hull FC I would imagine Herrington and his representatives went through all of these questions. Look, it’s Barcelona; it’s a difficult one to turn down, and they weren’t the only big club after him. But he’s only 18, and at his age, nothing is more important than playing football. His progression so far has been phenomenal – which is exactly why you don’t want that progression to be stunted, and that was the risk. He should play a fair bit of football for Hull, who are back in the Premier League for the first time in a decade. They have a very ambitious owner, Turkish media mogul Acun Ilıcalı, who decided to spend $24 million on Herrington, which could rise with add-ons. Clubs don’t do that for a player they intend to have sitting on the bench.

Advertisement

Hull have never finished higher than 16th in the Premier League, and it was a bit of a surprise that they got promoted last season through the Championship play-offs, so they undoubtedly face a challenge to stay up. But if you are good enough as a player, people will see it regardless of where your team sits on the table, and that’s the opportunity in front of Lucas now. Lucas Herrington in pre-season action for Hull City last week. Getty Images Playing as a centre-back for a newly promoted club means he will have a lot of defending to do. I actually think that could be good for him. He will make mistakes. He will have difficult afternoons. There will be strikers who expose parts of his game he still needs to improve. That is how you develop – and he does need to develop. Having said that, he’s obviously a fantastic player already: he’s very clever, a real modern-day centre-back who reads the game very well, and is comfortable with the ball at his feet. I saw him train with the Socceroos for the first time in March at Leichhardt Oval, when Tony Popovic first called him up. From day one, the kid did not look fazed by anything. He looked completely at ease. At the World Cup, it looked like he’d already played for the national team 50 times. He reminds me a bit of Harry Kewell when he first burst onto the scene with the Socceroos. They’re obviously different players – and Harry was a lot further down the line when he made his debut for Australia because he was already playing on and off in the Premier League for Leeds United – but I mean the way in which he’s been able to deal with the pressure and the expectation. It looks effortless, but we all know it’s not.

Advertisement

He has risen to every level so far: first in the A-League, then Major League Soccer in the US, the Socceroos and then the World Cup. Those are some big steps up, and nothing’s changed in his game. If he starts against Manchester United on Saturday night (9.30pm, AEST), as I hope and expect he will, he will be making another big step. This one is different. The Premier League is on par with the World Cup in terms of pressure, but now it’s more intense, because it’s 38 games plus all the cup competitions. A young Harry Kewell in 1997. Vince Caligiuri It’s going to be full-on for him. The attention of the world is on you as a player in the Premier League. Yes, that’s more for certain clubs than others, no doubt about it, but there is always a bit of a spotlight on the promoted clubs. And there will certainly be more pressure and more eyes on Lucas from Australia, too. That’s only natural. Related Article Analysis

Rory McIlroy has plunged the dagger into what many see as LIV’s lifeless form by questioning what value the likes of Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau have brought to the breakaway circuit. LIV is putting on its last tournament of 2026 this week and, despite claims of having an investor lined up, there are inevitably doubts about the league surviving into next year after the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund’s decided to pull funding. Rory McIlroy during a practice round for this week’s BMW Championships in Missouri. Getty Images Inevitably, focus has surrounded what will happen to the big names. It was revealed earlier this week that LIV executives are almost resigned to losing Rahm, regardless of whether funding remains a going concern. But after world No.1 Scottie Scheffler said he would see the positives in heavyweights such as Rahm – signed for US$300m ($421m) – and DeChambeau returning to the PGA Tour, McIlroy was far less compromising. The world No.2 went as far as to query whether the Tour really needs them back.

Advertisement

Jon Rahm tees off during day four of LIV Adelaide at The Grange Golf Club in February. Getty Images “I mean, have they brought value to LIV?” McIlroy said. “You know? I think the PGA Tour’s in a really good spot.” If Rahm found that answer difficult to hear from his Ryder Cup teammate, then McIlroy’s response on whether the LIV rebels would be welcomed home would not have been an easier listen. Brooks Koepka was reinstated immediately when he quit LIV at the end of last year – albeit with restricted appearances and a $5m fine – but Rahm and DeChambeau did not accept an offer on the same terms. “I’m pretty sure they’re not going to be welcomed back straight away,” McIlroy said.

Advertisement

“If they were offered this returning-member program back in February, the one that Brooks took, then, yeah, maybe. But that has sort of come and gone. And I think it was said at the time that the deal that they might get going forward isn’t going to be as good as the one that Brooks got. So, yeah, I would say it’s going to be a tough, tough road back.” McIlroy – who was talking at the BMW Championship in Missouri, which begins on Thursday – has been a vocal opponent of LIV ever since it was launched in 2022 and, despite some reservations, he is sticking to his guns if it does perish. Bryson DeChambeau and Rory McIlroy during the last round of the 2025 Masters. Getty Images “It’s a hard one,” he said. “I feel I’ve kept my position consistent that LIV has never been a good thing for the game. So, and whatever LIV 2.0 looks like, if it even happens, you know, they say they’re trying to be more collaborative and all that. But this is the [PGA Tour] is the best platform for the top professional golfers in the world. “And yeah, were there some things at the start of LIV that the PGA Tour could have done better? Sure. But you think back to the start with, say, Phil [Mickelson] being unhappy with some stuff. Like, surely that just warranted a conversation instead of blowing the entire professional game up and doing something else.

“So I don’t take any personal satisfaction in people losing jobs. That doesn’t seem right. I’ve always felt like this is the best place to play professional golf. And I’m pretty sure if the PGA Tour were handed $6 billion, it would have done a better job with it.” Related Article LIV Golf Series LIV Golf finds a lifeline investor but future of two biggest stars still uncertain Meanwhile, in Indianapolis, Scott O’Neil, the LIV chief executive, also talked to the media and admitted that time was running out to reach a deal with the potential investor. The bulk of the players committing to LIV 2.0 is critical. “We have a very compressed timeline to get the deal done,” O’Neil said. “I’m not going to share that here. But I can tell you we’re well on our way to a transaction. Look, the entirety of our focus is to get to this transaction and get through it. Without the players, that becomes very difficult. I have a good level of confidence in my conversation that we’ll have a critical mass of the right players to move this league forward.” The Telegraph, London

title: Cameron Green blew up at a Shield game. It was the moment he turned his Test career around
text:

SportCricketAustralian cricket Cameron Green blew up at a Shield game. It was the moment he turned his Test career around Daniel Brettig August 20, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Cameron Green has revealed how a low moment last summer became the point at which he finally nailed down the formula to become the Test batter that Australia desperately need him to be. Green, 27, made unfortunate headlines in March when he got into a press conference confrontation with a journalist following a Sheffield Shield game in Sydney, but he said on Thursday that the hundred he made that day was the moment he committed to a red-ball batting method to take back to Test cricket. Cameron Green celebrates his century against Bangladesh in the first Test in Darwin. Getty Images The hundred had followed a frustrating Ashes summer where Green often looked in an inordinate rush to make things happen, summed up by an ugly dismissal, backing away and bowled by England’s Brydon Carse at the Gabba. Australia were humbled by Bangladesh in Darwin last week, but Green’s second-innings century was proof that the mode of batting he settled on in March – so much so that he is revisiting the notes he made on that innings – is the right one for him.

Advertisement

“I went back to how I used to play, just keeping it really simple,” Green said. “Over the last few years I’ve tinkered a bit more to find something, tried to force it a little bit, so it was nice to go back to Shield cricket for a game last year, just went back to what I used to do and it felt really good. “I got a bit of clarity after that Shield game. It’s easy when you can go back to what felt good and what has worked well in the past. That’s basically all I really did. Loading “I’d normally like to be reasonably front on, bat on middle stump, just a really clear, simple game plan. Over the previous few tours or years, trying to get to off stump, trying to play a slightly more aggressive game early, rather than letting it happen. I think that’s the unfortunate thing but also the fortunate thing that I have been through it.” Recalled opener Matt Renshaw took up position at first slip in training drills on Thursday morning, with Steve Smith at second and Green’s fellow all-rounder Beau Webster at third.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket ‘Why are you out to get me?’ Green’s dummy spit raises questions ahead of $4m IPL stint Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer Green’s homework is also a result of his struggles to balance the competing demands of three formats, and a reminder that while he is currently batting in Travis Head’s former position at No.5, he does not have to bat like the freewheeling South Australian to succeed. “Travis Head is an unbelievable cricketer, and he seems to be a guy who can hit shots from ball one,” Green said. “That’s never really been me, so it’s just going back to what feels right for me, what I’ve done my whole life, and it felt nice the other day. “You try and write down notes because it’s a long time since we played a red-ball game, so I tried to write down a few notes from what worked in that Shield game. We had a World Cup, IPL, and some one-dayers in between, so it’s nice to go back to what did work, and try to remind yourself of that. “When you’re trying to force it, you want to do really well when you’re playing for Australia, sometimes you try to force those results, and unfortunately, in Test cricket you can’t score a hundred within 10 overs, you have to bat a few hours to get there, and when you feel like you’re forcing it, you’re trying to rush it too quick, so trying to get into that tempo that does work.”

Advertisement

As a shy young man who loves the comforts of his home in Perth, Green has thought about how to handle the challenges of near constant travel over the next 12 months. In 2023, Green played well on a Test tour of India, notching his first Test century, but trailed off later in the year as homesickness and fatigue took hold. This time around, he is likely to be accompanied by his wife-to-be Emily and other family and friends at various stages of the calendar, the better to feel happy and grounded even when he's thousands of kilometres away from home. Cameron Green at work in the nets ahead of the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay. Getty Images “It’s going to be a really tough 12 months, we’ve got the three hardest away tours, South Africa, India and England coming up as well as a World Cup, so it’s reasonably daunting, but also exciting for this group,” Green said. “We had a pretty similar schedule in 2023, and had a really successful year, so we’re hoping for the same. “[Tours] can be really exhausting, so it’s just taking it game by game, not looking too far ahead and just enjoying it. They can be really long tours and hopefully, you can drag your family across and just enjoy the moment.

Advertisement

“No one really enjoys being away from home for that long, so it’s kind of like bringing your family on the road and making that your new home.” Green looked at home in the middle in Darwin, the first time that has been the case in a Test match for a while. title: Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations
text:
Advertisement

InspirationGreat Ocean Road Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations Mex Cooper Updated August 20, 2026 — 11:09am ,first published August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s impossible to take the Great Ocean Road for granted: those sweeping ocean views at every twist and turn simply won’t let you. International travellers have made it Victoria’s most popular region for overnight stays, and Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements describes it as “one of Australia’s most compelling destinations”. But whether you’re crossing oceans to get here or you live close enough for a weekend getaway, it’s easy to stick to the same tourist stops. From off-grid retreats to sustainable dining, here are 10 ways to bypass the obvious and make travelling this spectacular stretch of bitumen a truly memorable experience. Get blown away Loch Ard Gorge lookout has stunning sights with fewer onlookers. The 12 Apostles rightly remain a must-see for tourists, even if there are only seven of the limestone pillars left. However, mere moments away, Loch Ard Gorge has similar stunning sights with fewer onlookers. Here you can delve into maritime history, including the famous shipwreck for which the gorge is named, before finding the blowhole lookout Poombeeyt Koontapool. Meaning “breath of the whale” in the Keerray Woorroong language, the elevated viewing platform allows you to hear the deep rumbles that precede crashing waves and the ocean whispers that carry calmer waters. Give the view time: watching it shift from serene to explosive can be mesmerising.

Advertisement

Sleep among the vines Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. A stay in the vineyard of Basalt Wines offers a snug cosy bedroom and stunning views. Two private villas set among the vines at boutique vineyard Basalt Wines (near Port Fairy), feel as luxurious as a 1920s boudoir with lush textiles and rich colours that entice you to curl up on the couch with a pinot noir. The only thing likely to draw you away is the cellar door restaurant, which pairs regional ingredients with Basalt’s own wines. Each villa has its own kitchenette, fireplace, deck, outside fire pit and breakfast hamper of local goodies. Killarney Beach and Tower Hill Wildlife Reserve are less than 10 minutes drive away. Wake to the ocean On clear nights, star gazing is unrivalled at Sky Pods.

Advertisement

Staying at Sky Pods makes you feel as if you have the edge of the ocean to yourself with 180-degree views across the Cape Otway coast. At dusk, a mob of grazing kangaroos hop into view before the sun sets over the Southern Ocean. Star gazing is unrivalled on clear nights but if too cloudy, a projector screen turns the luxury pod into a boutique cinema. This off-grid retreat, fed by solar power and filtered rain water, sits on 81 hectares of land being restored to its pre-farming state; 60,000 native trees have been planted over the past decade. A 20-minute walk down a bush track leads to Station Beach and access to the Great Ocean Walk, Aire River and Rainbow Falls. It’s a stay and view you will never forget. Meet the locals At Wildlife Wonders guides take groups through bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus and kangaroos. At Wildlife Wonders (five kilometres from Apollo Bay), expert guides take groups through protected bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus, kangaroos and many more. Visitors may be lucky enough to meet the rufous-bellied pademelon, a small wallaby-like marsupial that is extinct on the Australian mainland, or the even smaller long-nosed potoroo, while listening to the sounds of kookaburras, cockatoos and tree frogs. The 14-hectare sanctuary was established to raise funds for the Conservation Ecology Centre’s research projects. Dusk and dawn tours are available and in winter months there’s even a chance of spotting a migrating whale from the property’s commanding position. Feast from the sea

Advertisement

The Apollo Bay Fishing Co-op team with a fresh catch. No fancy five-star restaurant could compete with tucking into a freshly caught southern rock lobster at Apollo Bay’s Fishing Co-Operative. Since its establishment in 1948, the co-op has become a must for tourists and locals alike with its “ocean to plate” dining. The menu changes depending on the daily catch, but the true star is always there: grilled half rock lobster with garlic butter, chips and salad. The Apollo Bay harbour redevelopment shifted the co-op to a pop-up shop and separate fish market store, but both will reunite and return to their original and refurbished digs, including a new public viewing deck, by Christmas 2026. Go retro Angelsea’s The Monty sports a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. It’s only fitting that along one of the world’s best road trips, the classic roadside motel is being resurrected with a playful new vibe. Much like Australia’s original motor inns, Angelsea’s The Monty is inspired by American design, sporting a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. Mint-green walls, wavy mirrors, chequered bathrooms and bold orange accents bring the fun, while king-sized beds, curated mini-bars and coffee pod machines provide modern comforts. You can charge your EV or rent an electric bike. The lobby, which overlooks the Anglesea River, will morph into a new Mexican Cantina, Nina, to open in late 2026. It will feature a gluten-free menu with the right mix of sticky, tangy and fresh dishes with margaritas to match. The perfect spot to unwind after kayaking on the river or swimming at nearby beaches.

Advertisement

Ride a wave ... You may be surprised how far you go during a Go Ride a Wave surf lesson. Taking a surf lesson can feel daunting. There are the unpredictable waves, the ocean chill, the threat of rips, and the locals carving up the water, but halfway into a Go Ride A Wave two-hour class, and doubts begin to turn into a feeling you can do this. Some in your group may make it to standing, some to their knees, others stay flat, but most will likely leave surging with adrenaline and an urge to return. Supplied with a wetsuit, learner-friendly surfboard and plenty of expert guidance, the tutorial at famed Torquay beach is above all else exhilarating fun. … Then watch a pro Not a pro yet, but 13-year-old Leihani Zoric carves up a wave at Bells Beach’s Indigenous Surfing Titles in May. Justin McManus

Advertisement

Once you’ve realised just how tricky a pop-up can be, check out the masters at play as they weave through the waves at the Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach. The World Surf League Champion event, the longest running in competitive surfing, is held each Easter at the iconic beach. On days when the swell isn’t suitable, the action is halted but can provide the perfect opportunity to dive into Australia’s surfing culture and history at Torquay’s Australian National Surfing Museum. Enjoy a tasting tour Mediterranean-inspired deli Mortadeli serves sandwiches that demand your attention. Joe Armao The shared ingredient of the Great Ocean Road’s most delicious and diverse food is a commitment to quality seasonal produce. At the gateway to the road, the Booln Booln Cafe takes seemingly simple dishes such as sourdough jaffles and pastries and elevates them with native ingredients such as slow-cooked roo ragu and lemon myrtle meringue. At Aireys Inlet, cosy wine bar Le Comptoir invites you to while away hours grazing on a traditional French menu that incorporates local ingredients. Back in Torquay, Mortadeli, a Mediterranean-inspired deli and “caffeteria” serves seasonal soups, salads and pastas alongside its smash-hit sandwiches that demand both hands. Feed your soul

Advertisement

Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to charity. Bec Hudson And then there is one Surf Coast restaurant that is taking a really radical approach to sustainable dining. Torquay’s Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to local charity Feed Me, to help supply nutritious food to those in need. Using the food bank’s surplus vegetables, Samesyn transforms unwanted produce into critically acclaimed dishes, such as chewy carrots that are dehydrated then rehydrated in a carrot juice reduction and served with a maple sauce made from discarded Halloween pumpkins. There are no waiting staff, only chefs, who rotate through service shifts to share Samesyn’s mission – including achieving near zero waste – with customers. The nine-course tasting menu is a meal that will feed your soul. Related Article Great Ocean Road Australia’s wild and unforgiving coast makes this ‘great walk’ sublime THE DETAILS Visit

Wildlife Wonders offers a range of guided tours from $24-$75 for children and $59-$95 for adults. Family tickets and concessions available. See wildlifewonders.org.au. Go Ride A Wave in Torquay has two-hour surfing lessons for $84, wetsuit and surfboard hire included. See gorideawave.com.au/location/torquay. Stay

Dutch pianists Lucas Jussen, 33, and his brother, Arthur, 29, have been performing together since they were kids. Now regulars in the world’s top concert halls, they still share a room, and plates of food, on tour. Lucas (at front) and Arthur Jussen: “It’s very important that there’s not one boss,” says Arthur, “there must be a complete lack of ego in that way.” Marco Borggreve ARTHUR: Lucas is three-and-a-half years older than me, and when I came home from hospital, the first thing he did was hug and kiss me. That says something about the bond that was to develop; he accepted me straight away. He’s very easygoing and social, and I always played with Lucas and his friends when we were little. We slept in the same room, even though we each had our own; we could talk more. We still share a room when we’re on the road. We joke that if you go out with either one of us, you get the other brother, too. Thankfully, we like each other’s wives. Lucas has been with Annelise since he was 14, so I know her very well. I met my wife, Brenda, more recently. I’m a bit OCD. Lucas and Annelise bought an automatic vacuum cleaner and named it Arthur, so you can see how they mock me for that. I’m probably a bit square while Lucas is more spontaneous. If there was an important test, I’d start preparing a week before, whereas he’d do it all the day before. We’d end up in the same place, just via different methods.

Advertisement

Related Article Good Weekend At 14, Brett gave his sister a note and hid in the bathroom. Then she knocked on the door We really understand each other. One time, we were playing in Hamburg and, for some reason, I felt very nervous before going on stage. Lucas sensed this. Ten seconds before we went out, he said to me, “Look where we are; it’s amazing. Let’s enjoy it.” I instantly relaxed and we had a fantastic concert. Lucas had an especially busy year last year. He was moving house as well as performing a lot. I felt he was a little on edge, so I took on a lot of the admin that we usually share. I didn’t mind because I like to be organised and I knew it would just take something off his shoulders. We didn’t have to discuss it. We’re a very good team. If Lucas makes a joke on stage, I’m usually the first and loudest to laugh. What I find frustrating about him is also what I love. Lucas will give the receptionist or cleaning maid as much time as the boss; actually, he probably gives more to the maid. I really admire it but, sometimes, if you’re running late and he’s chatting for 10 minutes, you think, “C’mon!” But that’s just him; he’s very outgoing. We rehearse separately 90 per cent of the time and come together for the last 10 per cent. There’s no hierarchy when we play: it’s very important that there’s not one boss, there must be a complete lack of ego in that way. Every millisecond, I’m listening to what Lucas is doing and he’s doing the same, so who is leading can change within that millisecond.

Advertisement

When we’re sitting together [playing the same piano], I know when he wants to use one of the pedals, because I feel his leg gently touch mine. I know then to move mine away. That’s the easy thing about being brothers: you don’t have to bother saying, “When I touch your leg, it doesn’t mean I hate you.” We both like to work out and keep healthy and pretty much eat the same food; it’s not like one of us wants Chinese and the other Italian. We often get two plates of food, say a pasta and a salad, and share them. Even when it comes to music, we have the same tastes. We both like Frank Sinatra, Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder, Kool & the Gang, and Kylie Minogue. LUCAS: I can’t remember a time when I wasn’t with Arthur; I’d play more with him than with my own friends at school. We’ve asked our parents how we came to get along so well and they simply say, “It’s just luck; either you do or you don’t.” We certainly know siblings who really work on their relationships but don’t have the deep connection that we do. Arthur is a big dreamer – and I mean that in the literal sense. He’ll often have vivid dreams and talk in his sleep. One time, he woke me to tell me, “Calm down, calm down. It’s OK.” I woke up and said, “What’s the matter? I’m fine.” He looked me straight in the eye but he was fast asleep, probably dreaming.

Advertisement

Arthur likes to have structure in the way he approaches piano-playing and life; he likes to know what’s coming. He’ll be the one to fill in the visa forms. If a flight is delayed and we have to go on stage without a shower, I’d probably be easier about it than he would. I’ll be the one to say, “C’mon, it’ll be fine. We won’t smell as nice, but we’ll work it out.” The brothers have been performing together since they were children: “Every millisecond, I’m listening to what Lucas is doing and he’s doing the same,” Arthur says. @lucas_arthurjussen/instagram In terms of our looks, Arthur’s hair is more styled, whereas mine’s a bit wild. He’s more into fashion trends than I am, too: I tend to be a bit more classical. And he loves perfume. There’s a duty-free shop at Amsterdam airport with a huge fragrance section. We fly out of that airport two or three times a week and he would’ve been in that shop 300 times. He’s gone deep down the scent rabbit-hole and I don’t think he’s ever coming out. We spend more time apart from each other now that we’re both married. Last year, I spoke out because we’d done more than 100 concerts and I wanted to pull back on the intensity of that. Arthur wasn’t in the same headspace as me; he wanted to keep going. The difference [in what we wanted] was only small, but things came to a head. We talked it through, though, and met in the middle. He came to realise later that pulling back a bit had been good for him, too. I really admire Arthur’s drive to be the best he can be every time we go on stage together; he has a big tank in that way. It’s inspiring to have someone beside you who can deliver that drive all the time. If I’m having an off day, it pulls me through.

Faith-based schools in Melbourne’s growth corridors are among the fastest-growing private educators in Victoria, with school leaders attributing the boom to parents favouring schools that reflect their religious values. Of the top 20 private schools that have recorded the biggest enrolment jumps over the past decade, more than half are faith-based – eight Islamic and five Christian – The Age’s analysis of enrolment data shows. Islamic schools such as Al Siraat College are among the fastest-growing private schools in Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Al Siraat College in Epping has grown by 911 students in the past 10 years – an increase of 142 per cent. Most of the school’s students were born in Australia, with their parents or grandparents migrating mostly from the Indian subcontinent or the Middle East. Collectively, the school’s families speak 39 languages other than English.

Advertisement

The expansion has brought growing pains, which deputy principal and co-founder, Rahat Arain, credits staff for managing “like a beautiful garden, growing”. “We are bursting at the seams, and trying to have our infrastructure play catch-up with the growth,” she said. “The pressures from the community wanting to enrol in an Islamic school have driven up the class sizes. That’s something that we then address through extra support staff in the classroom. This adds pressure to staffing to make sure that we have what’s required for a growing school population.” At school, all students learn Arabic and participate in prayers. Islamic teachings are also incorporated into the curriculum.

Advertisement

“For example, when we’re looking at civics and citizenship, you can look at it from a faith-based perspective as well,” Arain said. Al Siraat College co-founder and deputy principal Rahat Arain, who has seen the school grow by 900 students in the past decade. Ruby Alexander “What does our creator say about how we should be living a civic life? How does that compare to the opportunities we’ve got in Australia and democracy, and so forth. “Obviously, every school brings its own flavours, but I think our parents are looking for that overlay of how does it relate to who I am as a Muslim and how can [my child] access the curriculum?” The Australian International Academy of Education in Coburg – which opened in 1983 after a donation by then-king Khalid of Saudi Arabia and claims to be the oldest Islamic school in the country – has added 950 students in the past decade. The increase followed the opening of a new campus in Caroline Springs in 2014.

Advertisement

The Coburg campus, which has added 270 students in the past decade, recently opened a new multimillion-dollar building housing a prayer room and year 11 and 12 classrooms, and is nearing capacity, said campus head Michelle Shears. “Families are increasingly choosing faith-based schools because they are seeking an education that supports not only academic achievement, but also the development of strong character, values and a clear sense of identity,” Shears said. Many former students are now enrolling their own children at the school. “Their decision to return with subsequent generations demonstrates a level of trust and confidence that has been built over time,” Shears said. “Alongside new families joining our community, these generational connections contribute to our continued growth.”

The demographic picture is different at Heathdale Christian College, where most families are first-generation Australians, says executive principal Ross Grace. The school, which has campuses in Werribee and Melton, added 1151 students in the past decade – the seventh-biggest jump in enrolments statewide. “A number of our families who are first-generation Australians, when they were kids themselves they were in a Catholic school in South Asia, and so those schools were built on the foundations of values, and they were good schools that they remember well and want the same for their children,” Grace said. title: Forgot Book Week? Emergency costumes that require zero craft skills
text:
For some, Book Week is one of the most magical annual events in the Australian calendar – a time-honoured tradition stretching back generations (since 1945, specifically), where kids and their caregivers come together to get creative and celebrate their favourite stories and characters. For others, it’s just another tedious task that puts pressure on time-poor parents to whip up whimsy from their already-drained resources. Sometimes, it’s a bit of both.

There’s no doubt that, as with many other things, the rise of social media has seen the expectations around Book Week costumes soar, with the twin thieves of joy – competition and comparison – leading many parents to want to give up altogether or worse, pull out the Elsa and Woody costumes from the bottom of the dress-up box and call it a day.

The point of Book Week is, of course, to put books front and centre, and the costume frenzy can sometimes cause that to get lost. Because as much as kids might want to be a Disney princess or K-Pop Demon Hunter, it defeats the purpose (unless, of course, their primary point of contact for those characters is the book versions – in which case, break out the purple braids!).

It’s hard to keep up with the never-ending homework assignments of parenthood. But Book Week is a great opportunity to take a moment to connect with kids if you let the books lead the way, rather than the costumes. Going to the library or your home bookshelves and combing through them with your kids, having conversations about their favourite stories and characters, is far more important than any elaborately styled outfit.

Then, when it comes to the actual dressing up, it doesn’t have to be complicated. Adapting everyday clothing and household items you already own can be part of the fun – and online hubs like Facebook Marketplace are a great additional way to simplify the process, whether that’s by finding completed costumes that are being offloaded from Book Weeks past, or reusable items and materials you need to complete your kids’ looks.

title: From royal exit to return: The story behind Harry and Meghan's Atlantic crossing

In brief Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will move back to the UK soon, British press reported.

It follows a tumultuous six years in the United States.

Six years after stepping down as working royals, Prince Harry and his wife Meghan Markle are moving back to the United Kingdom within weeks, British press reported on Thursday.

In a surprise move, Harry, the youngest son of King Charles III, and his wife "plan to leave the United States by the end of the month to settle in a private, non-royal residence, which is said to be located outside London", The Telegraph reported.

Several UK news outlets, including the BBC, reported the couple's two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, had already been enrolled in a British school for the start of the school year in early September.

It was reported that the couple had already chosen a new house, but that it would not be one of the many royal residences.

Harry and Meghan have lived in California since stepping down as working royals in 2020 and the children had not seen their grandfather Charles since 2022.

Harry, 41, and Meghan, 45, left the UK for North America in 2020 amid a bitter feud with his family, which worsened as Harry published his tell-all memoir Spare.

A no-holds-barred interview with US talk show host Oprah Winfrey also deepened the rift.

The BBC said the 77-year-old Charles had been made aware on Sunday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex planned to return to live in the UK.

The monarch welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity, but there will be no expected change to the couple's official status, the BBC reported.

Why the move back?

While no official reason for the move has been shared, the news comes only weeks after Harry and Meghan paid a short visit to the UK in early July with the children, during which they had a private meeting with Charles.

Harry said last year that he wanted to reconcile with his father, who was diagnosed two years ago with cancer and has been receiving treatment since. The type of cancer has never been revealed.

It was not immediately clear whether Harry's older brother and heir to the throne, Prince William, and his wife, Catherine, had been told of the news. The two brothers have become estranged and reportedly no longer talk.

The UK's Sun newspaper reported the couple would keep their Montecito home in California.

While the couple signed a mega deal with Netflix in 2020 — reportedly worth an unconfirmed US$100 million ($140 million) — many of their projects have struggled to win over audiences.

The new deal signed with the US streaming giant in August 2025 was a looser arrangement, described as a "multi-year, first look deal".

A timeline of Harry and Meghan's time abroad

In January 2020, Harry and Meghan announced they would step down as senior members of the royal family and work to become financially independent. They moved in June that year to California, where Meghan was born and raised.

In 2021, Markle told Winfrey in a bombshell interview that she faced racism from a member of the royal family while she was pregnant with Archie, saying an unnamed person raised concerns about "how dark his skin might be". In the same interview, Harry said his father no longer took his calls.

She was pregnant with their second child at the time of the interview, and Lilibet was born in June that year.

The couple were visiting London in September 2022 when Queen Elizabeth died, and they stayed for her funeral.

In 2023, Harry published his memoir, which detailed his relationships with his family members.

Among the most notable revelations, Harry says his brother William, now heir to the British throne, knocked him to the floor during a 2019 argument at his London home over Meghan.

William called Meghan "difficult," "rude" and "abrasive", Harry said. He also said he and his brother had asked their father not to marry Camilla Parker Bowles, who is now Britain's queen.

Harry attended his father's coronation in May 2023 without Meghan, but did not sit with other senior royals.

In February 2024, Buckingham Palace announced that King Charles had been diagnosed with cancer. The following month, William's wife, Kate, announced she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy after cancer was detected in tests.

Last year, after losing a legal challenge over the level of security he was entitled to in the UK, Harry said he could not see a world in which he would bring his wife and children back to the country.

But he said he would "love a reconciliation with my family".

"There's no point continuing to fight any more, life is precious," he told the BBC at the time.

Upcoming anniversary of Princess Diana's death

News of the couple's surprise return after their painful departure from Britain — dubbed Megxit by the British tabloids — also comes the day after Diana's brother, Charles Spencer, revealed that he had written a book about his sister's life.

Harry has long blamed the media for the death of his mother Princess Diana, who was killed in a Paris car crash in 1997 while trying to shake off the paparazzi.

There was an outpouring of grief across the UK following the death of Princess Diana in 1997. Source: Getty / Jon Jones/Sygma

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister will be published in Britain and other countries on 22 September and translated into 12 languages.

"With the 30th anniversary of Diana's tragic death on the skyline, I've been inundated yet again with requests for interviews about my sister," Spencer said.

"This has convinced me to write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all," he said, adding many opinions were "based on untruths that have become accepted over time".

Spencer, 62, has remained close to both his nephews, and Harry and Meghan and their children reportedly visited the earl's ancestral home at Althorp, central England, in early July, where they were said to have visited Diana's grave.

title: Here's which Centrelink payments are going up and by how much

Pay rates for non-resident single pensioners will increase by $5 a fortnight, while partnered non-resident pensions will increase by $1.70 a fortnight each.

What JobSeeker recipients will receive

For singles without children who receive JobSeeker payments, the highest rate increases by $16.20 to $833.70 every two weeks. For singles with dependent children, the rate will increase by $17.30 to $892.80.

The rate for couples will rise by $14.80 per person, bringing the fortnightly payment to $763 each.

Changes to parenting payment rates

Parenting payment recipients will also see an increase, with maximum rates rising by $20.90 to $1,087.20 fortnightly for singles and by $14.80 to $763 for partnered recipients.

Rent assistance to increase

One million renters will also receive increased Commonwealth Rent Assistance rates.

The maximum rent assistance will increase by $4.40 per fortnight for singles without children, bringing it to $223.80. Singles with one or two children will see a $5.18 rise to $211, while those with three or more children will get a $5.88 boost to $297.36.

The maximum payment for couples without children will increase by $4.20 to a combined rate of $211.

For couples with one or two children, the increase is $5.18, bringing the combined total to $263.06. For those with three or more children, the increase is $5.88, bringing the total to $297.36.

Youth Allowance payments are also rising

For those aged 18 to 24, youth allowance will increase by $20.90 to $1,087.20 from 20 September.

ABSTUDY rates to increase

Single Australians aged 22 or over receiving ABSTUDY with no dependent children will see their fortnightly payment rise by $16.20, bringing it to $833.70. Those with dependent children will see a $17.30 increase, taking their fortnightly payment to $892.80.

The payment for those aged 55 and above without dependent children will increase by $17.30, bringing it to $899.80.

For people aged 22 or older who are partnered, the ABSTUDY payment will increase by $14.80 to $763, whether or not they have children.

What else will change?

Alongside these indexation increases, the government has lifted social security deeming rates.

Deemed rates are used to calculate income from financial assets and to assess eligibility for government payments.

From 20 September, the deeming rate will increase from 1.25 per cent to 1.75 per cent for financial assets up to $66,800 for singles and $110,600 for couples combined.

For all financial assets exceeding the threshold, the rate has risen by 0.5 per cent to 3.75 per cent.

title: Can you access your super early? Australia's rules and exceptions explained
text:
In brief Accessing your superannuation early isn't common, but it can be done.

But what are the rules for doing so? And should you do it at all?

Australians are sitting on about $4.4 trillion in superannuation savings for retirement. But there are ongoing debates about whether they should be allowed to access some of that money early to help with costs of living.

And making an early withdrawal can have a big potential impact on your future retirement savings — especially if you are in your 20s or 30s.

So what are the rules around early withdrawal, and who do you have to convince if you're making a claim?

Strict rules on early access

Superannuation savings are intended to help people cover their living expenses when they have left the workforce and are in retirement.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taxes on super contributions are lower than income tax rates, and withdrawals after retirement are also at discounted tax rates.

Those low tax rates come with strings attached: rules that prevent people from using their superannuation savings for other reasons than income in retirement.

For the most part, superannuation savings in Australia are not readily withdrawn until at least age 60. People can withdraw super from age 60 if they have stopped working, or from age 65 even if they have not stopped working.

The Australian Taxation Office is very clear that there are limited circumstances in which you can access your superannuation before retirement:

on a range of compassionate grounds (such as for medical treatments, funeral expenses and preventing a forced sale of your home)

a terminal medical condition

severe financial hardship

temporary or permanent incapacity to work.

But the rules are strict. And who you need to apply to will depend on your reasons for seeking to withdraw money.

For instance, if you apply on compassionate grounds, you need to apply via the tax office and meet all of its criteria.

READ MORE Labor reveals super increase position amid 'predatory' practices crackdown

But in other circumstances, such as severe financial hardship, you need to apply directly through your super fund. Even if you meet all the criteria — which includes having received government income support payments for at least half a year — it's up to the fund trustees' discretion whether to say yes. The most you can withdraw for severe financial hardship is $10,000 in one year.

People often wish they could access their super for help with house deposits or home loan repayments. First home buyers may be eligible for the First Home Super Saver scheme. But in general, just needing help for mortgage repayments is not going to be sufficient grounds to access your super savings.

Beware scams and misleading ads

The tax office has had to issue warnings about misleading ads and social media claims, encouraging people to try to withdraw super on compassionate grounds, such as medical or dental expenses that are not absolutely necessary on health grounds.

The tax office says to be particularly careful with anyone suggesting super can be accessed to pay for cosmetic or elective procedures, as these treatments usually aren’t eligible.

If someone offers to help you apply to your super fund to take money out, that’s a red flag. It could even be a scam.

You can report ads or social media accounts making misleading statements about early access to super, either online or by calling the tax office’s tip-off hotline: 1800 060 062.

Separately, unlicensed, real-time "cold calls" about superannuation will soon be banned, under consumer protection law changes announced by Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino on Wednesday.

READ MORE There's another reason to check who inherits your superannuation

These rules will aim to prevent scammers or salespeople encouraging people to move their super, as happened with the First Guardian and Shield funds which later collapsed, affecting almost 12,000 people and around $1 billion in retirement savings.

Consider the long-term savings hit

There are lessons from the COVID pandemic about why withdrawal rules are so strict.

In 2020, the Coalition government's COVID-19 Early Release Scheme allowed participants in financial hardship easy access to up to $20,000 from their super because many Australians were doing it tough.

One of us (Susan) was involved in a 2023 study that combined data from one of Australia's largest super funds, Cbus, with a survey of more than 3,000 of its members to examine why people withdrew some of their super savings.

A majority of people reported they did need the money immediately. But around one quarter (26.6 per cent) said they were anticipating future needs.

Almost half (48.5 per cent) said they thought about the decision for a week or less, while many also withdrew as much as they could. When asked about the impact on their long-term retirement savings, only 17% correctly estimated how large an impact it would have.

By the end of 2020, 3.5 million Australians had made at least one successful application to withdraw from their super accounts, totalling about $38 billion.

A 2024 Super Members Council analysis of the COVID Early Release Super scheme found that a person aged 30 who withdrew the full $20,000 could be expected to retire with about $93,600 less in superannuation.

Protecting retirement funds

There will always be arguments for freeing up access to super a little.

But it’s important to keep the primary objective of the superannuation system firmly in sight.

The system exists to help finance the dignified retirement of working Australians, together with other sources of support such as the Age Pension, in an equitable and sustainable way.

title: Irene was Australian born. So why did she need this certificate to return home?
text:
At Steven Law's home in Northcote, Melbourne, family albums are strewn across the dining room table, offering glimpses into a past that was rarely discussed.

A large sepia photograph catches Steven's eye and he lifts a magnifying glass to look more closely.

It features a woman — Steven's grandmother Irene Law — wearing a large hat and a scarf draped around her shoulders. It is just the way Steven remembers her.

"Irene was an elegant woman; she was well spoken, well dressed. That was how we knew her," Steven told SBS Chinese.

Decades after her death, her image has appeared on walls across Australia, as part of artist Peter Drew’s Aussie poster series — bringing a little-known chapter of her life into view and raising questions about who gets to be called Australian.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Aussie 'paradox'

When Steven's sister Christina Law discovered that her grandmother would feature in Drew's poster collection, she was moved to tears.

"I was really overwhelmed and quite teary when I saw that nanna had been included in this series," Christina told SBS Chinese.

The posters feature archival photographs, sourced from the National Archives of Australia (NAA) of people who applied for certificates exempting them from the dictation test.

Under the Immigration Restriction Act 1901, one of the laws that formed part of what is now known as the White Australia policy, the dictation test could be administered at an officer's discretion to people seeking entry to Australia.

It required a person to write a 50-word passage in a European language dictated by an immigration officer. After 1905, the officer could choose "any prescribed language", making it possible to administer the test in a language the person did not understand.

People who failed were declared a "prohibited immigrant" and refused entry or , in some circumstances, deported.

The exemption certificates were designed to allow eligible non-European residents who had lived in Australia to leave temporarily and return within a set timeframe without being subjected to the dictation test.

People applying for the exemption from the dictation test were generally required to demonstrate they were of good character and produce written references. Source: SBS News / National Archives of Australia

It's been more than a decade since Drew debuted the poster series in 2016.

The posters have since sparked mixed reactions, including graffiti, counter-posters and attempts to tear them down.

In recent months, videos of the artworks being defaced and altered to include different messages about identity have also circulated on social media.

"Someone has vandalised my old posters, so I've got some new ones, and I'm going to fix them up," Drew told SBS Chinese while standing on Morphett Street in Adelaide's central business district.

He's equipped with a canvas rucksack full of supplies and replaces the graffitied artworks with the ease of someone who has installed thousands of posters over the years.

Peter Drew has spent more than a decade producing, installing and often replacing his iconic Aussie posters. Source: SBS News / George Chan

Asked whether the "Aussie" label on his posters is a question or statement, Drew said there's no simple answer.

"In some ways, the posters have a double meaning because the first way to read it is that the person in the poster is Aussie, and that's a celebration of them being Australian," he said.

"But in another way, the poster is also saying that the White Australia policy is Aussie, and that's something that we don't celebrate. So, there is a paradox because those two things are conflicting with each other."

For Steven and Christina, the posters illuminate a chapter of their family's history that remained largely shrouded in secrecy.

'We knew nothing'

In 1900, Irene (then known as Lucy Maud Lem Cue) was born in South Wangaratta in north-east Victoria.

Her biological mother was born in New Zealand and had British ancestry. Her father, Lem Cue, was of Chinese descent and died when Irene was two years old. She was then adopted by another Chinese-European family and raised in Melbourne.

At the age of 18, Irene travelled to Hong Kong with her adoptive father, who hoped to recruit workers for his furniture manufacturing business and expand his commercial interests in China.

In March 1921, she returned to Australia and obtained a Certificate Exemption from Dictation Test (CEDT) before travelling back to Hong Kong.

Irene would eventually marry and raise children — mostly on her own, after her husband's death.

In the 1970s, Irene returned permanently to Melbourne, where she remained until she died at age 80.

READ MORE A dark chapter of Australia's past is resurfacing in immigration politics

Despite her overseas travels, Irene was born in Australia and therefore considered a British subject by birth (Australian citizenship was later introduced in 1949). That legal status, however, did not necessarily protect people of Chinese and other non-European backgrounds from immigration restrictions.

But historian Michael Williams believes people of Chinese ancestry were "overwhelmingly" targeted by Australian immigration officials during this period.

"Legally, yes, they were definitely Australians. But socially, it was a bit more problematic," Williams told SBS Chinese.

"If they grew up looking Chinese, then they would not have been considered Australian. The White Australia policy pretty much identified an Australian as being a white person."

Michael Williams has long studied Chinese-Australian history, including the impacts of the White Australia policy. Source: SBS News / George Chan

When Steven discovered that his grandmother's records had been preserved by the NAA, he felt a "stronger" connection to his family's past but admits he also felt angry.

"Irene never spoke to us about the difficulties she had. We knew nothing about that until after she passed away.

"We were a bit angry in a way, that these people were Australians; they were Australian-born, yet they needed these documents in order to return to the country."

The White Australia policy and its legacy

According to the NAA, only a "small number" of people were granted CEDTs. Those exemptions could allow non-European residents to travel overseas and return to Australia, while those who were not exempted could face exclusion.

The dictation test was administered 1,359 times before 1909, with only 52 people granted entry, according to the NAA. After 1909, no migrants required to sit the test passed.

Williams said he has seen examples of dictation tests in which immigration officers targeted people from multicultural backgrounds who understood English.

"If you happened to speak English, they would test you in Greek or Estonian at one stage ... and as a result of failing the test ... you were [considered living] illegally in Australia and could be put in jail."

READ MORE Those in Australia feel the shift. Those outside are watching closely

The dictation test was abolished in 1958, but elements of the White Australia policy remained in place for years afterwards. The final remnants of the policy were removed in 1973, while the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 subsequently made racial discrimination unlawful in areas covered by the legislation.

Christina said she learnt about the mechanisms of the White Australia policy at school, but for a long time, did not realise how this history personally impacted her.

"I see now that it relates to me. I mean that was why we were the only Asian family in the school because no other Asians were allowed into the country at the time."

It was not until the 1980s, after Irene Law's death, that Steven and Christina started researching their family history. Source: SBS News / George Chan

Steven also remembers questioning his Australian identity at a young age.

"People called us names, we were teased, and we often felt isolated," he said.

Now 66, Steven said he feels "richer" because of his Chinese ancestry and cultural traditions passed down through generations.

His experience reflects a broader shift in the makeup of Australian society. About 731,500 people born in China lived in Australia in June 2025, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

The 2021 Census recorded more than 1.39 million people with Chinese ancestry, making it one of the largest overseas-born ancestry communities in the country.

When people from multicultural backgrounds walk the streets and spot Drew's brightly coloured posters, he hopes they are reminded that Australian identity "has room for them".

"It's not such a rigid thing that is set in the past and static, not evolving. It's actually ... much stronger ... than that."

Steven also believes the artworks continue to send a powerful reminder that people, no matter their background, are "welcome here, no matter where they're from".

"[Irene] was Aussie, just as much as we are. Just as much as the other people in the posters."

title: 'Left feeling like a burden': How the government's new NDIS changes may impact you
text:
In brief The government says its NDIS changes will save billions of dollars.

Advocates aren't convinced, saying the changes have left disabled Australians feeling like a burden.

An overhaul of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) has passed the Senate with Coalition support, sent back to the Labor-controlled lower house to be rubber-stamped.

Analysis by the Grattan Institute suggests hundreds of thousands of people will be moved off the scheme or prevented from joining under the changes.

Applicants will be assessed in stages under a new test to determine their functional capacity.

That test is still being developed and will replace the current diagnosis-based model.

Acting CEO of peak body People With Disability Australia Megan Spindler-Smith says her community is grieving.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"There will be harm, there will be injuries. What we're talking about here is that when you reduce people's access to the supports that they need to be able to get out of bed, access the community, go to work, you ostensibly isolate people."

She says many lives will be made smaller by the reforms — which will slash social and community participation supports in half.

"The support needs don't go away when the funding is cut or when the supports are removed. They just get pushed onto either systems or other people, and that means isolation."

Since it started in 2013, the cost of the scheme has ballooned, rising to $50 billion dollars this year, and projected to hit $100 billion within a decade.

The government says its overhaul will slow the scheme’s growth and save almost $38 billion over the next four years.

Greens MPs like Jordon Steele-John say the focus on financial cost has made many disabled people feel like a burden.

“Many people, during the course of this debate, while the government has been trying to push this legislation through, have shared with me that they have felt as though they are being talked about in a way that leaves them feeling like a burden, and that is just not okay.”

Health Minister Mark Butler says reining in spending growth was necessary to safeguard the scheme's financial sustainability and social license.

"This plan puts the scheme back on track, and I'm confident, secures it for decades to come," Butler said.

"It genuinely has transformed the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, and I want to continue to see that happen for decades to come. But we know also that we need to build supports for people who were never intended to be covered by the NDIS, people with more low to moderate support needs, those sorts of second-tier supports that were envisaged by the designers of this amazing reform."

After a snap Senate inquiry that received more than 4,500 submissions, amid sustained campaigning from advocates, the government cut a deal with the Coalition to pass the bill.

A total of 63 amendments were tabled across both houses, but Disability Program Director at the Grattan Institute Sam Bennett says those that passed are only minor in scope.

"I wouldn't say any of them are particularly significant, in all honesty. I think mostly they're pretty minor tweaks to the existing provisions within the Act. Many of them probably done by government to try and clarify their existing drafting.”

READ MORE Controversial NDIS changes get last-minute green light as Labor cuts deal with Coalition

The Coalition secured amendments to create new fraud offences, including penalties for NDIS providers that offer inducements or kickbacks.

The legislation also includes clearer guidance on what supports parents are expected to provide, clarifies rights to request re-assessment, and boosts whistleblower protections.

After pressure from the Greens, the government added to explanatory material clarifying a requirement for applicants to seek all appropriate treatment before being eligible for the NDIS.

Spindler-Smith says it was a significant win.

"What we now have is some really strong clarification that things like restrictive practices, and that's anything that limits the rights and freedom of movement for people with disability — and that could include seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint, or environmental restraint — those things are being clarified that they are not part of that because in theory, they could fit under all appropriate treatment."

"And the requirements for someone to access the NDIS would have been really problematic if they had been one of the requirements under the all appropriate treatment."

Another amendment clarifies the scope of ministerial powers that will allow social and community supports to be cut, while safeguarding other supports for participants with the highest needs.

READ MORE Government admits NDIS reforms will impact families, downplays fears over state readiness

"We see that as something that will make sure that people who do require 24-hour support and care are not going to be impacted in the same way, because there were some real concerns," Spindler-Smith said.

The focus will now shift to programs being created by the states and territories, which will be responsible for providing alternative supports from January 2028.

They'll be funded through a five-year, $10 billion commitment, split evenly between state and territory governments and the Commonwealth.

Most advanced at this stage is Thriving Kids, a $4 billion program for children with mild to moderate autism and developmental delays.

It’s meant to start in six weeks, and preparedness varies by jurisdiction, but despite agreeing in principle, Queensland is yet to sign up.

Butler says he remains confident alternative supports will be put in place.

"That's the deal that we've struck with states and territories," Butler said. "Thriving Kids is well underway. Implementation plans have been agreed with all states and territories except Queensland, which frankly needs to get its act together. But all other states and territories have implementation plans in place to build them. They'll be in place before the before the first of January, I'm very confident."

But he acknowledges much of the design and delivery of this overhaul is yet to come.

"We have a ton of work to do on other population groups, so kids over the age of nine, adults with more low to moderate support needs. We've got a lot of work to do with states and territories, but we've got time to do that. We've got the commitment of all states, premiers and chief ministers signed that deal with the prime minister earlier this year. We've got money allocated. We now just have to get on with the job."

A technical working group will provide advice to government on the new assessment tool this year and into next.

The new legislation is due to undergo statutory review within five years.

title: Why a 52-metre SpaceX rocket ended up off the coast of Christmas Island
text:
In brief A SpaceX rocket splashed down off the coast of Christmas Island.

Residents delighted at the arrival of the 52-metre rocket, lining up to see it towed to shore.

Elon Musk's aerospace company SpaceX has retrieved a rocket that splashed down in the Indian Ocean near Christmas Island.

The space debris was towed to the remote island, about 1,500 kilometres off north-west Western Australia, on Tuesday.

"After approx. 24 days at sea, the SpaceX Recovery team successfully guided Starship to a location just off the coast of Christmas Island," the US aerospace manufacturer and launch services company said in a social media post.

"A team of SpaceX engineers is on their way to conduct additional analysis on the vehicle in calmer waters before attempting to return it to Starbase."

Locals in the remote territory reportedly lined up along the rugged coastline to catch a glimpse of the 52-metre-long rocket as it was towed in.

Photographer Chris Bray, who usually focuses on wildlife, said it was not something he ever expected to see.

"This SpaceX Starship was towed into the protected waters around Christmas Island this morning after an unusually gentle landing in the Indian Ocean almost a month ago left it unexpectedly floating and potentially recoverable instead of the usual explosion!" he said on an Instagram post on Tuesday.

"Cool to see! So BIG!"

Bray's aerial photos show the mostly black-coloured rocket being towed by cable attached to two large ships.

title: Labor reveals super increase position amid 'predatory' practices crackdown
text:
In Brief The government ruled out lifting compulsory super above 12 per cent as debate over retirement savings grows.

Labor will crack down on lead generators accused of steering Australians into high-risk investments.

Labor will not increase how much superannuation employers must pay workers, instead focusing on reforms to stamp out "predatory" practices used to lure people to put retirement savings into risky investments.

The superannuation guarantee rate — the minimum percentage of a worker's earnings that employers must pay into a retirement fund — is 12 per cent, and there have been calls within Labor to raise the rate to 15 per cent.

While rebuffing the need to increase the guarantee rate, the government has doubled down on its defence of the superannuation system amid calls from One Nation to allow workers to withdraw funds before retirement to help pay off mortgages.

"There's no plans to lift the super guarantee," Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino, who unveiled the long-awaited consumer protection reforms on Wednesday, told ABC's Radio National.

He said raising the rate to 12 per cent was something Labor had long pushed for and that was now "putting people in a very strong position" for retirement.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Mulino detailed the long-awaited crackdown on predatory practices in an address to the National Press Club on Wednesday, after the high-profile collapses of First Guardian and Shield Master Funds in 2024 and 2025 stripped an estimated 12,000 Australians of their retirement savings.

The reforms land in the middle of a wider fight over superannuation.

One Nation has pushed to loosen rules around early access, while the government ruled out any rise to the compulsory super guarantee on Wednesday morning.

What's changing?

The reforms target "lead generators" — operators who use social media, online ads and cold calls to funnel people's retirement into high-risk schemes.

Unlicensed real-time communication about superannuation will be banned, and licensees will be required to take reasonable steps to ensure lead generation activities comply with legal requirements.

The anti‑hawking regime will also be bolstered, with stronger consent requirements, a narrower exemption for financial advisers to existing clients, and harsher penalties for breaches.

Mulino said the reforms were designed to strengthen consumer protections and disrupt "predatory and inappropriate behaviour" that led to the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian funds.

"Lead generators reaching out to these people in unsolicited ways, undertaking highly manipulative interactions to convince them that their super products were not performing well or were inappropriate, and then manipulating them into inappropriate products for them," Mulino told ABC radio on Wednesday morning.

READ MORE A troubling new record as Australians' financial woes surge

The government previously floated the measures in a consultation paper published in April.

The Financial Advice Association of Australia (FAAA) has previously called on Labor to crack down on the practices, which can steer consumers towards inappropriate financial products.

FAAA chief executive Sarah Abood said the collapse of Shield and First Guardian showed how devastating high-pressure sales tactics can be when unregulated.

"Around 12,000 Australians lost, in some cases, all their retirement savings after being targeted by sales processes that looked and felt like advice," Abood said.

"Consumers need stronger protections against predatory lead generation, while still being able to find the right adviser for them."

SBS' The Feed spoke to victims of the collapses in July 2025, including Melbourne woman Susy Zjak, 52, who lost her entire $574,000 super balance after being cold-called and steered into the First Guardian Master Fund.

"I felt dizzy. I just cried. I vomited. I actually thought I was going to have a heart attack. It was the worst nightmare of my life," Zjak said at the time. "This is 30 years of working, 30 years of hard working."

A new political battleground

The reforms come as superannuation threatens to become a fresh political battleground.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson called this week for super rules to be relaxed and allow Australians to withdraw their super during the cost of living crisis, labelling the current system as broken.

READ MORE When should you be able to access your super? Battle lines are being drawn

Treasurer Jim Chalmers rejected the idea on Tuesday, warning it would "absolutely decimate the retirement incomes of millions of Australian workers" and that One Nation was undermining the superannuation system.

"One of the most important features of our superannuation system is ... this idea that, with compounding interest over time, Australian workers can access the decent retirement incomes that they need and deserve after a lifetime of work."

Australian Council of Trade Unions president Michele O'Neil backed that view on Wednesday morning, but said people shouldn't be forced to choose between surviving now and their future retirement.

"Workers shouldn't have to choose between housing and being able to have a retirement with some dignity and not retiring into poverty," O'Neil said.

"We have to recognise that it's a good thing that we've built up the opportunity for people to be able to retire with a bit of security — it shouldn't be an either-or.

"We need to keep super strong and growing for people. If money's taken out early, then they get less at the end. They don't get all that compounding effect, which is so important when you face retirement."

READ MORE The $400k super line that could define how comfortable retirement is

Currently, super can only be accessed in limited circumstances, such as stopping the foreclosure of a home, a terminal medical condition or severe financial hardship.

Tax office figures show 67,900 early super releases were approved in 2024/25, amounting to just over $1.4 billion.

Of those who had withdrawn money from their super, 43 per cent said they regretted it. Source: SBS News

New research from comparison site Finder found 24 per cent of Australians have withdrawn money from their super before retirement, according to a survey of 1,011 people.

Medical expenses were the most common reason, cited by 9 per cent, with another 9 per cent withdrawing for "other reasons". Eight per cent did so during the COVID pandemic, and 4 per cent have used their super to help fund a house deposit.

Eleven per cent said they were considering a withdrawal, while 65 per cent said they had no plans to touch their super early.

Of those who had accessed their super early, 43 per cent said they regretted it.

title: Want lower energy bills? You might want to skip this popular upgrade first
text:
In brief Australians are keen to electrify their homes.

But many are making the wrong moves when starting that process.

Many Australians want to go fully electric. But it’s often hard to know where to start. Solar? A home battery? Or quitting gas?

To find the best way to make the shift, we modelled three pathways for a three-bedroom house in Melbourne’s western suburbs.

These pathways show it’s important to do things in the right order. It’s best to start by lowering energy demand through better insulation and stopping draughts, and then switch from gas heating to an efficient reverse-cycle air conditioner. Home batteries should ideally be done last.

What did we do?

We used benchmark data to model a household with ducted gas heating, gas hot water and cooktop, common electric household appliances and a petrol car.
