Each year this household uses 5,300 kilowatt-hours of electricity, just under 50 gigajoules of gas, and about 1,230 litres of petrol (to drive 11,100 kilometres). This costs $2,477 for electricity, $1,494 for gas and $2,255 for petrol. Total energy costs are $6,226 a year.

We modelled replacing these with a 10-kilowatt ducted reverse-cycle air conditioner, a hot water heat pump and an induction cooktop.

We also modelled two further options: one where the household switches to a mid-range EV with a battery of about 60kWh and another where the household keeps its petrol car.

Which pathway?

We tested three pathways to going electric. These don’t include rebates or the cost of the EV.

Pathway 1a – all electric, no battery, EV

Here, the household adds a large 11.76kW solar array, gets off gas and replaces its petrol car with an EV.

Although total electricity use rises, the grid electricity bill falls due to solar. The new electricity bill would be about $1,800. Because gas and petrol costs fall to zero, the household saves about $4,400 yearly.

Total cost: about $32,600.

Pathway 2a – all electric, medium home battery, EV

This pathway mirrors the first, but adds a 13.5kWh home battery at the end. The power bill falls to about $950. Savings would be about $5,300.

Total cost: about $48,100.

Pathway 3a – all electric, large home battery, EV

Here, the household doubles storage to 27kWh. The power bill drops to about $600. It doesn’t reach zero due to low solar over some periods and annual supply charges. Annual savings: about $5,900.

Total cost: about $56,400.

Stacking rebates

These figures combine the prices in Victoria's

official guide

with

advertised price benchmarks

for installed appliances as of June 2026. The hot water heat pump is costed after an upfront discount. These pathways don’t directly hold for other regions, due to factors such as climatic difference and government incentives.

Governments offer a range of rebates and subsidies for households to go electric.

Federal incentives

Pathway 1: Applying a solar rebate means the cost falls to just under $30,000.

Pathway 2: Using solar and battery rebates, the cost falls to about $41,700.

Pathway 3: After both rebates, the cost falls to $47,800.

State rebates

In Victoria, the maximum possible state support comes to just over $6,000.

This includes $1,400 for solar, $1,400 for locally made hot water, and indicative discounts of about $2,500 to replace ducted gas with a 10kW reverse cycle air conditioner, $560 to switch from gas hot water to electric and $140 for induction cooktops. These are maximums, not entitlements, and there are eligibility requirements.

If the household was eligible for all federal and Victorian rebates, the total cost would fall to about $23,900, $35,800 and $41,800 for the three pathways, respectively.

Electrify in the right order

Our modelling suggests an optimal order for going electric.

1. Reduce demand

The first step is making the house more energy efficient by sealing gaps, boosting insulation and adding shading to stop direct sun. This can make it possible to install smaller appliances.

2. Go solar

Solar is a no-brainer almost everywhere. When choosing the size, it’s best to go bigger to power a future all-electric home.

In Melbourne, a 11.76kW array would produce about 15,400kWh a year. Set hot water systems, appliances and EV chargers to run during the day to maximise use of solar. Our modelled all-electric household with an EV uses 8,500kWh a year in total, including 1,800kWh for EV charging.

3. Get off gas

First, replace expensive older gas heaters with a correctly sized reverse-cycle air conditioner. This will bring immediate savings and can also cool in summer.

Next, replace gas hot water with a quiet, efficient heat pump.

Then replace gas cooktops with induction. These can be expensive, so consider trialling a portable induction hob. Finally, abolish the meter.

4. Consider a battery

Batteries should only be installed if they are useful. The most common use is releasing stored power from solar to avoid peak evening rates.

Home batteries are more valuable once gas appliances and petrol cars have been replaced and the home is fully electric. In our model, the first battery saves about $852 a year, while doubling storage saves only another $355 a year. This is why they should be done last if possible.

How quickly does this pay off?

Unlike other home improvements, householders can often recoup the cost of going electric. But payback time differs a lot. Quitting gas can rapidly pay itself off, while oversized home batteries can take much longer.

For our three pathways for a household with an EV, simple payback takes 5.4, 6.8 and 7.4 years respectively. Zero- or low-interest loans offered by some governments can reduce upfront cost, but will push payback time back roughly 2–3 years.

To optimise payback, it’s best to begin by improving the building to reduce energy use, shift away from gas to efficient electric appliances, use solar directly if available and then buy a home battery if warranted.

title: 'Front agents' at centre of latest unlawful migration crackdown
text:
in brief In three separate cases, registered migration agents allowed unregistered people to provide migration assistance.

Only registered migration agents, Australian legal practitioners and exempt persons can lawfully provide immigration assistance in Australia.

Australia's migration agent watchdog has vowed to remove "fake agents" from the profession following multiple cases of unlawful immigration assistance.

The Office of the Migration Agents Registration Authority (OMARA) has sanctioned three registered migration agents in what the government described as an "ongoing crackdown".

Julian Hill, the assistant minister for citizenship, customs and multicultural affairs, said the government is strengthening immigration oversight.

"When people pay a migration agent they rightly expect a qualified person will do the work, not an untrained, unregistered fake agent," he said in a government statement on Tuesday.

"No one would put up with people borrowing registration numbers from doctors, lawyers or financial planners and neither should they when hiring a registered migration agent."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The three cases form part of a broader regulatory push by OMARA.

OMARA's monitoring team was established in October and "proactively monitored" 85 registered migration agents during 2025-26, identifying 43 instances of non-compliance and addressing them through education, engagement and regulatory action, according to the government statement.

"Alongside the Investigations team, which examines allegations of serious misconduct, OMARA sanctioned 28 registered migration agents in 2025-26," it added.

'Front agents'

In three separate cases, registered migration agents permitted unregistered individuals to provide migration assistance under the agents' Migration Agent Registration Numbers (MARNs), a practice commonly referred to as "front agent" activity.

In the first case, an agent’s registration was cancelled after OMARA determined that hundreds of visa applications submitted through three business ImmiAccounts involved either undisclosed immigration assistance or assistance provided by staff who were not registered migration agents.

ImmiAccount is the Department of Home Affairs' online portal for lodging and managing visa and citizenship applications.

READ MORE The major citizenship ruling affecting Australians like Ophelia

In the second case, an agent was suspended after acknowledging that his son, who was not a registered migration agent, had provided immigration assistance on the business's behalf.

The investigation also uncovered allegations that clients had received falsified departmental correspondence intended to give the impression that visa applications had been lodged when they had not.

In the third matter, an agent was suspended after knowingly permitting another business director to lodge visa applications using the agent’s MARN while the director worked towards becoming a registered migration agent.

The government said it has strengthened OMARA's regulatory capability, with the regulator now using both investigations and proactive monitoring to improve compliance and professional standards.

OMARA said in the release that bad actors will be identified and "removed from the profession".

"While the vast majority of RMAs [registered migration agent] act with integrity and professionalism, there is a small cohort who intentionally seek to undermine the migration program for personal gain," it said.

"These actors bring the migration advice profession into disrepute and tarnish the reputation of those RMAs who do the right thing in the best interests of their clients."

Only registered migration agents, Australian legal practitioners and exempt persons can lawfully provide immigration assistance in Australia.

Consumers can check whether an agent is registered through the migration agents register.

title: Behind One Nation's 'gayest party' claim lies a long and complex history
text:
IN BRIEF MP Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation, arguing the party is not homophobic.

Researchers say the party has work to do on getting voter support from the community.

Can a political party whose past and current members have described LGBTQI+ people as having a "mental illness" be one of the "gayest parties" in Australia?

It's a question provoked by recent comments from One Nation members in the past week.

When asked about former WA One Nation candidate Parminder Singh's comments — first reported by the ABC, that gay people have a "mental illness" — federal MP Barnaby Joyce rejected them as "highly offensive".

"We're one of the gayest parties in Australia," Joyce added.

But some of Australia's most prominent LGBTQI+ activists and equality campaigners say the party has more work to do in convincing the community it's truly living up to that title.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's probably fair to say the community’s reaction has been a mixture of confusion and incredulity," Equality Australia legal director Heather Corkhill told SBS News.

"It's not every day you have politicians from the same party declaring both that being gay is a mental illness and that they are the gayest party in Australia, all in the space of a week."

'We're not homophobes'

Singh — who has since apologised for his comments — isn't the only one to have said members of the LGBTQI+ community have a "mental illness".

In comments first reported by The Guardian, One Nation WA senator Tyron Whitten said during a podcast interview segment about 'gender' in August last year that "there's male, there's female, and then there's mental illness".

"If you want to wear a dress, that's fine. I don't care. But ... they can't keep saying that, 'Hey kids, that's normal'," he added.

"You're going to be a boy or you're going to be a girl. And parents that are promoting this, I think that's child abuse."

SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment on the remarks.

Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation, arguing the party is not homophobic. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Joyce is adamant the party is not a "pack of homophobes", describing that as a "vindictive trope" against One Nation.

"We're not here to glorify, we're not here to vilify. We're here for people to live their own life," he said on Tuesday.

'Positions deeply hostile'

Jordan McSwiney, a senior research fellow at the University of Canberra, says while One Nation may accept the existence of the community, it "certainly doesn't embrace this community".

McSwiney listed past positions, votes and policies of the party on LGBTQI+ issues, including Joyce and Hanson personally opposing same-sex marriage and abstaining from the 2017 parliamentary vote, the party's opposition to the now-abolished Safe Schools program, and what he described as its "anti-trans" politics, and "homophobic" remarks by current and former members.

Earlier this year, One Nation's South Australian leader Cory Bernardi doubled down on past comments linking same-sex marriage to bestiality, saying his position had not changed.

In 2019, Hanson rejected a parliamentary motion to recognise intersex people, asking: "How many more of the 39 categories do we have to consider in this parliament? I just think it is ridiculous." She recently took aim at "transgender ideology" that she said was "infecting society".

In 2017 she sought to move an amendment to a draft law to protect civil celebrants who wanted the right to refuse to marry gay couples, saying: "I don't believe we are fully aware of the ramifications this is going to have on our society."

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson publicly opposed same-sex marriage and abstained from a parliamentary vote in 2017. More recently, she said LGBTQI+ people should keep their sexuality "behind closed doors". Source: AAP / Jay Kogler

While she initially indicated she would vote in support of the marriage equality bill if Australians backed it, she ultimately abstained.

Corkhill says recent Senate bills and motions including the abandoned Sex Discrimination Act reforms, along with rhetoric about a "transgender insurgency" indicate many in the LGBTQI+ community "are still being targeted by efforts to roll back their rights and further marginalise them".

"You can't on the one hand claim to not be homophobic while retaining positions that are deeply hostile to the broader community, such as trans rights and opposing reforms that would end legal discrimination against gay students and staff in religious schools."

McSwiney said while One Nation accept some parts of the community, that may not extend to others, including transgender Australians.

When asked about the party's stance on the transgender community, Joyce said it's a matter of personal spaces.

"As a father of four daughters, they don't want to find someone in their change room who's a bloke," he said.

At the same time, Hanson has a history of condemning some members making homophobic remarks.

Hanson and the party's former NSW leader Mark Latham had a falling out after Hanson labelled his homophobic slur toward a fellow MP "disgusting", and urged him to apologise. Another candidate was dumped by Hanson in 2017 for saying "gays should be treated as patients".

The party also includes members of the gay community. Its latest parliamentary recruit — South Australian MP Jason Virgo — is a gay man who once campaigned for marriage equality, and its national director, long-time staffer James Ashby, is also a gay man.

Corkhill says voters will judge political parties by their policies, their candidates and whether they’re willing to stand up for equality, "not by the sexual orientation of some of their members".

"Having gay members isn't the same as defending gay people's rights and tolerating same-sex marriage isn't the same as supporting the equality of the whole LGBTIQ+ community."

'I still don't like it'

While One Nation may have evolved in its position on marriage equality to accept the status quo, some things have not. Hanson stands by her infamous "I don't like it" remark in regard to Mardi Gras, saying people should keep their sexuality "behind closed doors".

McSwiney says One Nation's approach to the LGBTQI+ community has similarities to its stance on migrants — not celebrating, but tolerating them.

"They claim the 'right gays' ... are the ones who just quietly go about their business and work hard, which is not dissimilar to the way they talk about migrants in this country," he said.

"I guess you could say it's quite an assimilationist, like a hetero-assimilationist approach as well to the LGBTQIA community in Australia. They tolerate that these communities exist, but they're certainly not embracing it to be proud of it."

Can One Nation win the pink vote?

The LGBTQI+ community, like every other, is not monolithic — and it may be that other One Nation policies and positions may win over voters.

"If nearly 30 per cent of the electorate is voting for One Nation, I'm sure that includes members of the LGBTQIA+ community," McSwiney said.

"(But) I certainly wouldn't say that they're like a top focus group target. And they're probably not going to win or lose seats on the back of that community."

Human rights scholar Paula Gerber says the party still has work to do to win votes.

"Just saying 'we're the gayest party', I don't think is a vote winner. It's about the substance that sits behind that assertion," Gerber said.

"Unless there's some significant recognition of how hurtful and offensive those positions and those comments are to the LGBTIQA+ community, an apology and a promise to do better in the future, I can't see that the LGBTIQ+ community is going to feel comfortable voting for that party."

title: Controversial NDIS changes get last-minute green light as Labor cuts deal with Coalition
text:
In brief Controversial NDIS changes have passed the upper house.

Despite last-minute amendments and outcry from advocates, the government struck a deal with the Coalition.

Dozens of eleventh-hour amendments to a controversial bill designed to claw back runaway disability spending have passed the upper house despite outcry from advocates.

Labor has been touting changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme, including sweeping new powers for the relevant minister and a cut in social funding, since April in a bid to save $37.8 billion by the end of the decade.

The changes passed the Senate on Tuesday night, with 28 in favour and 12 against.

But just hours before a final vote on the bill was due to take place, the government unveiled 63 changes in response to community concern.

Under one change, severely disabled Australians who require constant care will be able to appeal decisions made by the NDIS minister that affect their funding.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Participants can request a variation to their plan for specific sections, including assistance with daily living.

Community and social participation funding, which is set to be slashed despite its role in helping disabled people access friends, appointments and work, will remain ineligible for appeal.

The changes to the scheme would take away a lifeline for thousands of Australians, Greens disability spokesperson Jordon Steele-John said.

"Labor and the Liberals got together in a room, and they decided to strip us of our rights, regardless of our safety and dignity," said Steele-John, who lives with a disability.

Increased penalties for NDIS providers benefiting from kickbacks have been included in the changes, along with specific whistleblower protections.

"There will be tough new aggravated integrity offences, including obtaining funds by deception, providing false or misleading information for abuse of position as a participant's nominee, or for intentionally destroying records," NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister told reporters before the amendments were voted on.

The changes passed the upper house on Tuesday night with little debate, following a deal struck with the coalition for the removal of a so-called widow tax hidden in the federal government's budget reforms.

In exchange for closing the loophole, which would have caused divorcees and widows to lose negative gearing entitlements on investment properties, the opposition will support Labor's bill.

The conflation of the previously unrelated topics rendered disabled people a political football, Steele-John said.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers had announced Labor's plans to close the loophole weeks earlier, but the government was not planning to introduce it to parliament until later in 2026, with consultation on the draft bill not due to end until Friday.

READ MORE Government admits NDIS reforms will impact families, downplays fears over state readiness

With the NDIS laws marooned in the Senate, the government's promised budget savings were eroding each day the package was not passed.

Chalmers initially claimed there was no rush to pass the tranche two reforms because the changes only applied from July 2027.

But pressure ramped up on Labor to move faster on the widow tax fix after independent senator David Pocock revealed he had been contacted by a domestic violence victim who claimed she had been denied financing on a property because of the loophole.

The tax reforms grandfathered negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions for investors who held property before budget night, including for landlords who jointly owned a property with a spouse.

However, if their marriage broke down or their spouse died, they would lose their negative gearing entitlements when the title transferred to their name, under the initial legislation implementing the reforms.

title: Designed to 'exploit' children: Meta faces a historic courtroom reckoning
text:
In brief US states accused Meta of knowingly designing addictive platforms that harm youth mental health.

Prosecutors are demanding $282 billion in penalties in a historic landmark federal trial.

Meta knowingly hooked and exploited children, a United States federal court has heard in the trial of the social media giant on charges that it deliberately made Instagram and Facebook addictive to young users.

In what many experts have called social media's "big tobacco moment," a coalition of US states is demanding Meta pay US$200 billion ($282 billion) in penalties for using technology specifically designed to foster addiction among children in a similar fashion to cigarettes.

Meta "exploited how kids' brains work," California prosecutor Megan O'Neill said in opening arguments, painting Meta's business model as one built to "hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public".

"It worked especially well for kids," O'Neill added. "Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe."

Meta's lawyer, Paul Schmidt, acknowledged that some users were harmed by the networks, but argued that the company had "tried to come up with tools to help them". He argued research showed no clear link between adolescents' social media use and a lack of well-being.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He also said Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's co-founder and CEO, shared the company's desire to improve its services, and not make them dangerous.

"They don't believe they're going to do well if people don't like their service," Schmidt said.

Before the trial began, the company denied all the allegations, insisting it had worked with parents, experts and law enforcement to incorporate protective safeguards for children.

Mothers rally

This is not the first case seeking to hold tech companies — including Meta — accountable for these types of issues, but it could become one of the most consequential if it leads to sweeping changes on the platforms.

Meta founder and chief Mark Zuckerberg is among the star witnesses expected to testify, along with Instagram head Adam Mosseri.

Family members hold a banner with the names of nearly 400 young people who allegedly died from the impacts of social media outside a courthouse in Oakland, California. Source: AFP / Godofredo A Vasquez

Activists, including mothers of children they say were driven to suicide by their social media usage, rallied outside court.

One mother, Lori Schott, called out Zuckerberg and Mosseri, saying they "built one of those most powerful and richest companies in the world... But power does not excuse harm."

First of many?

This is the first federal trial in what is expected to be a tidal wave of lawsuits also targeting TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube as families, educators and state governments charge them with harming the mental health of young people.

Meta, which has more than three billion users worldwide, is the sole defendant in this case.

In addition to financial penalties, the states are demanding changes to Meta's apps to protect young users, including limits to screen time.

Four states — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — are representing a coalition of 29 states that first sued Meta in 2023.

The charges are three-fold: that Meta lied to the public about how dangerous its apps are for minors; designed some features specifically to get them hooked and stay online, including screen time-limiting ones that are easy to get around; and gathered data on children under age 13 without parental consent, in violation of federal law.

The trial is expected to last six weeks, with a verdict expected by October.

For Meta, "the huge issue here is reputational harm" and being forced to make major changes to its social media platforms, Vincent Joralemon, a director at Berkeley's Life Sciences Law and Policy Center, told the Agence-France Presse news agency.

Experts see parallels with a three-decade-old settlement between dozens of US states and tobacco companies.

"It really feels like tobacco in the 1990s," Joralemon said.

While cases about social media harms revolve around the intersection of technology and addiction, the case against Meta focuses on its business practices, similar to when US regulators sued tobacco companies, Joralemon said.

Dozens of US states sued four major tobacco companies for downplaying the harmful health impacts of their products, and won a 1998 landmark settlement that included financial penalties and changes to product marketing.

Those tobacco companies have paid over US$176 billion ($248 billion) since, according to data from the National Association of Attorneys General.

title: Here's what's set to change as gambling and 'widow tax' reforms partly greenlit
text:
In brief Gambling ads will face tougher restrictions, including a new opt-out register.

Betting inducements and direct marketing will also face new limits.

Contentious gambling reforms, including restrictions on incentives and a national register to opt out of online gambling ads, are set to pass after Labor and the Coalition struck a deal.

The Labor caucus approved the deal on Tuesday morning, after the government made several amendments to secure Coalition support.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the reforms would protect those most at risk of harm.

"Australians will be better protected from inducements and direct marketing," he told parliament.

But gambling reform advocates have been critical of the bill, which was passed in the lower house with 96 votes to nine. It will be debated in the upper house and is expected to be passed this week.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Among them were two Coalition MPs — Pat Conaghan and Andrew Wallace — who crossed the floor and joined the independents to vote against the laws. Both have spoken out, saying the laws don't go far enough.

"I don't like gambling. The reality is $36 billion is lost on gambling each and every single year. That's $95 million a day that is lost to gambling in Australia," Wallace told News24.

"I've never crossed the floor in 10 years in my parliamentary career but I've just heard too many stories of my constituents and people across Australia who have lost everything, who have sometimes lost their lives."

READ MORE Government unveils last-minute gambling reforms ahead of critical new report

The agreement between the government and Opposition means the Coalition will also support changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) in exchange for Labor expediting a push to remove a so-called widow's tax which was part of tax changes in the May budget.

What are the gambling amendments?

More than a dozen amendments were made, including:

A gambling advertising blackout extended to 15 minutes before games

A ban on ads during children's programming

A start time on 'three-per-hour' broadcast restrictions moving from 6am to 5am

Banning direct marketing for 14 days after signing up to a betting company

Banning direct marketing to high-risk customers

Banning direct marketing for 90 days after a person deregisters from BetStop

Ban commissions for any staff or affiliates of gambling companies

Mirroring live sport restrictions for broadcast to online services

The establishment of a register, allowing Australians to opt out of seeing online gambling ads. The register will be made up by betting companies

The laws will be reviewed three years after they take effect.

Who are the reforms' supporters and critics?

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government had listened to the community and taken steps to address the "most toxic version of inducements".

"The reforms introduced to parliament represent the most significant reforms to online gambling in Australia’s history," she said.

"This package of reforms minimises children’s exposure to wagering advertising, takes action on predatory inducements and cracks down on illegal gambling operators."

Opposition communications spokesperson Sarah Henderson claimed the amendments were a win for the Coalition.

"Labor's bill simply did not go far enough to protect children and vulnerable Australians," she said.

"Sport time is family time and our amendments strengthen those protections."

The gambling reforms are the first in the three years since a landmark report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy, who called for a total phase-out of gambling ads.

A Senate committee report on the proposed changes was tabled on Monday night, criticising the government's reforms as being too little, too late.

It contained criticism from the Coalition, the Greens, and independent senator David Pocock, and pointed out that many of the Murphy report's recommendations were not included in the legislation.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young slammed the major party leaders for "throwing Peta Murphy's legacy out the door".

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young was among the critics of the reforms. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"And what have we got from the leader of the Opposition? 'Oh, okay, prime minister, whatever you say, prime minister.' I mean, how pathetic," she said.

Hanson-Young said Opposition leader Angus Taylor had blindly followed the prime minister, likening him to Albanese's dog Toto.

Albanese thanked the "parliament for coming together on this issue".

The Greens had called for a complete ban on online gambling advertising and the establishment of a national regulator, both of which have not been included.

Pocock, a longstanding gambling reform advocate, accused the government of backing in gambling companies and shafting the Australian public.

"It is no surprise where ... we have a Labor Party tie itself in knots for three years ... and then they get Angus Taylor to negotiate one-on-one with the PM and come to some sort of gentlemen's agreement," he told the Senate.

Closing of a 'widow tax' loophole

Labor and the Coalition also reached an agreement to remove a so-called widow tax, which would have caused divorcees and widows to lose negative gearing entitlements on investment properties.

The loophole was included in the federal government's budget tax reform.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers had agreed to close it, but not until later in the year.

That has been brought forward under an agreement with the Coalition, who will support Labor's bill to slash spending on the NDIS.

title: A 'huge' trade-off: One Nation's pitch for cheaper cigarettes
text:
In brief One Nation has proposed slashing the tobacco tax by 75 per cent to address the surge in black market activity.

Experts are divided on whether cheaper cigarettes would weaken organised crime networks or undermine decades of tobacco control efforts.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has vowed to slash the tax on tobacco by 75 per cent and dramatically reduce the price of legal cigarettes, arguing the move would curb the booming black market.

Illicit tobacco trade in Australia has expanded rapidly since 2020. The value of illicit tobacco attempting to enter the market has soared from $1.74 billion in 2018-19 to more than $6.4 billion in 2023-24, according to Australian Taxation Office estimates.

Meanwhile, government revenue from the tobacco excise — the tax applied to legal tobacco products — has plummeted and is forecast to continue declining.

"Labor has not only lost the revenue, it has lost control of the black market in illegal tobacco," Hanson said in her announcement on Tuesday.

Hanson said her party would also pause indexation on the excise for three years, saying the policy, if passed through in full, would reduce the price of a $46.50 legal packet of cigarettes to around $21 to $22.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Tobacco is subject to a high excise to keep prices high and discourage smoking. Currently, excise duty rates increase by 5 per cent each year, in addition to routine indexation.

"This is not about encouraging smoking. It is about restoring the rule of law and breaking the black market," Hanson said.

Labor has previously resisted calls to cut the excise. On Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was not considering a cut and its focus was on compliance.

What could a policy like this accomplish? Experts have mixed views on how it would impact crime, public health and government revenue from the excise.

The public health perspective

The use of illicit tobacco has surged in recent years, raising alarm bells for public health experts despite an overall decline in smoking rates.

Laura Hunter, CEO of the Australian Council on Smoking and Health, told SBS News making cigarettes cheaper would have "huge ramifications for the health of Australians".

"Australia now has the lowest smoking rates that we've ever recorded, and that's the result of decades of policies that are designed to make cigarettes less affordable, less available in the community, and less normalised," she said.

Source: SBS News

Hunter rejected the idea that legal tobacco prices were the primary driver of the black market, arguing its growth was being fuelled by international organised crime networks mass producing illicit tobacco.

"Our tobacco laws in Australia were never designed to combat sophisticated organised crime groups," she said.

She said crackdown measures across the country, including efforts to strengthen tobacco laws and enhance on-the-ground enforcement, were starting to turn the tide, and urged state and territory governments to continue tightening legislation.

She also disputed the argument that lowering the excise would hinder the illegal market's price advantage.

"You can't price match criminals," she said.

Last year, the Australian Medical Association's president said calls to reduce the excise were "misguided" and backed by big tobacco.

"There's absolutely no evidence to support the idea that reducing excise will impact illegal tobacco — in fact the evidence says the opposite," Danielle McMullen said.

"Jurisdictions that have reduced the excise [are] seeing a horrible combination of increased smoking rates and no tangible impact on the illegal tobacco trade."

Tobacco use carries serious health risks and is a leading cause of preventable illness and death.

How could it impact revenue?

Legal cigarettes now cost upwards of $40 a pack, with the excise accounting for the bulk of the price.

The revenue from the excise increased steadily until 2020, when it began to fall from a high of $16.3 billion to $7.8 billion in the 2024-25 financial year.

Analysis last year from the e61 Institute, which describes itself as a not-for-profit, non-partisan economic research institute, found cutting the tobacco excise might not be enough to draw smokers back to legal products, and could worsen government revenue declines.

Even if legal cigarettes fell to around $21 a pack under One Nation's proposal, they would still be substantially more expensive than many illicit products.

Fei Gao, a taxation lecturer in the University of Sydney's School of Accounting, Governance and Regulation, told SBS News it's "too late" to cut the excise, and any such move would have needed to occur several years ago.

"I don't think it's going to be an incentive for people to switch back to the legal product," she said. "When the customers are gone, they're gone. They will only go back if you can beat the price."

Gao said the likely result would be an even faster decline in government tobacco excise revenue.

Australia, a world leader in smoking reduction measures, introduced graphic health warnings in 2006 and pioneered plain packaging laws.

Gao noted that legal tobacco manufacturers face costs that illicit operators do not, making it difficult to compete on price with black-market products.

A criminologist's view

James Martin, associate professor in criminology at Deakin University, studies the illicit tobacco trade. He argued the growth of Australia's black market was primarily driven by tobacco excise increases.

He said organised crime groups had captured a growing share of the market by offering much cheaper products, while government efforts to tackle the trade through enforcement have yielded limited results.

"We've seen massive investment in law enforcement over the last few years, and it's been accompanied by record arrests, record seizures," he told SBS News.

"But the actual impacts on the market have been negligible."

Martin said reducing the excise could shrink the illegal market and lure consumers back into regulated channels, arguing that criminal groups would be unable to compete with the efficiency of legal manufacturers.

While public health advocates warn cheaper cigarettes could increase smoking rates, Martin notes that illicit tobacco is already widely available at low prices across Australia.

He said enforcement would remain important, but would not be effective until a "critical mass of consumers" could be diverted back to the legal market.

title: Women’s physical and mental health 'inseparable', new endometreosis research finds
text:
in brief Almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.

One in three women experiencing mental health issues are not seeking help.

Women living with endometriosis, ovarian cysts and hormone-related conditions are experiencing significantly higher rates of anxiety, depression and self-harm, highlighting the need for mental health support to be integrated into women’s physical healthcare.

Research published by Women's Mental Health Australia on Tuesday found almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.

Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome experienced depression and anxiety at up to twice the rate of women without the condition.

The findings have uncovered major gaps in Australia's healthcare system, according to chief operating officer Katrina Locandro.

"It's enormous," she told the Australian Associated Press.

"The government's investing a lot in women's health at the moment ... and there is a really practical step that they could be taking to reduce that gap."

The findings indicate that physical health conditions are associated with poorer mental health.

But the greatest psychological toll is on women living with female-specific physical health conditions, including polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, a broad condition involving a hormone imbalance, irregular periods and ovarian cysts.

Women with that syndrome reported high rates of depression and anxiety, between 1.6 and 2.2 times higher than women who did not have the condition.

The disparity also extended to suicide and self-harm rates, reported by 10 per cent of women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and 13 per cent of women with endometriosis, compared with four per cent of women without those conditions.

The research found that one in three women are not seeking help for their mental health issues, often because of financial and stigma-related reasons.

Locandro says every woman attending a government-funded endometriosis and pelvic pain clinic should receive an integrated mental health assessment and support as a standard offering.

"We're not asking the government to build a new system, we're asking it to strengthen an existing one by recognising that women's physical and mental health are inseparable," she said.

Report co-author Bronwyn Graham said that embedding integrated mental health assessment and support into existing services would be a game-changer.

"Women are being asked to manage two separate journeys, one for their body and one for their mind, and to find their own way between them at the point they are least able to."

title: A high-stakes vote on wealth, power and inequality is looming
text:
In brief California will vote on a proposed wealth tax in November.

Home to many billionaires and their companies, the proposed tax has many supporters — and powerful critics.

In November, California will vote on a proposal to levy a one-off 5 per cent tax on the wealth of all billionaires in the state.

Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin has already spent US$100 million on political donations to a group opposing the tax. Brin is hoping to avoid a potential tax bill of US$13 billion, a return of roughly 130-to-1 if that investment is successful.

Advocates of the billionaire tax claim it would raise US$100 billion in revenue, to be allocated directly to state-funded healthcare, food assistance and public education.

Supporters of the union-backed proposal also highlight that most billionaires currently pay lower marginal rates of tax than the average worker, and that the revenue is desperately needed to fill gaps in funding created by US President Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid.

Its critics, which include California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, argue the measure will drive billionaires and their tax revenue to leave the state.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taxing the ultrawealthy

Similar measures targeting the ultrawealthy are currently under consideration around the world.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed a 2 per cent income tax increase for those earning over US$1 million, and passed a property surcharge tax on second homes. Other US states — including Washington state, Maine and Minnesota — have passed or are considering similar income or wealth tax measures.

In the United Kingdom, a group of 120 millionaires have launched a “Proud to Pay” campaign asking the government to levy an additional 2% tax on wealth over £10 million.

Spiralling global inequality

Behind the public discussion of California’s billionaire tax lies a much deeper debate about spiralling global inequality.

Recent data from the US shows the share of economic output flowing to workers has dropped to a record low of 52.9 per cent in 2026. This means for every US$100 the economy produces, workers take home US$52.90 in pay, the smallest share since records began in 1947.

Similar trends have been observed around the world.

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

Conversely, the wealth of billionaires has accelerated rapidly. As of 2026, Forbes reports a global record 3,428 billionaires.

Perhaps most symptomatically, in June Elon Musk briefly became the world’s first trillionaire after the public launch of SpaceX. His wealth now sits at around US$800 billion.

The causes of inequality

Some blame globalisation for this explosion of inequality, but there are two other important related factors to consider as well.

The first is the global decline of the trade union movement. With union membership and power declining around the world, the ability of workers to negotiate for better wages has declined.

The second is a trend of corporate consolidation into a small number of large superstar firms. These companies, which include tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Uber, wield monopoly-like powers. This reduces competition and allows these firms to drive down wages.

The rise of artificial intelligence and automation will only accelerate these trends, enabling the largest firms to shed even more workers even as the firms’ output and profitability continues to climb.

Workers feel the crunch

For the last couple of decades, stagnating wages have been propped up by cheap access to credit. With central banks using unconventional policies to keep interest rates low, household spending has remained largely stable, funded by an increase in household debt.

However, with inflation rising, central banks around the world have pushed up interest rates from emergency lows during the pandemic, cutting off the source of cheap credit. With inflation rising faster than wages, the effect has been real declines in living standards.

Unsurprisingly, voters are unhappy at this “cost of living” crisis, and all over the world have turned away from incumbents and established parties.

A jump to the left?

If the previous decade’s politics have been dominated by dissent on the right, many countries are now seeing the emergence of stronger dissent on the left.

After Mamdani’s headline-grabbing victory in New York, Democratic Socialists have ridden a wave of momentum to win a series of primary races. Beyond the US, we can note left-independent Catherine Connolly’s election as Irish president, the rise of the Greens in the UK, and the recent resurgence of left-wing Die Linke in Germany.

These different parties and leaders all share a focus on combating growing global inequalities of wealth and power. Billionaires, the most obvious and visible symbol of global wealth inequalities, are an obvious target.

However, as California’s proposal shows, attempts to rein in the wealth and power of billionaires should expect furious backlash from billionaires themselves.

In addition to Brin’s US$100 million, other billionaire donors including Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt and Chris Larsen have also spent significantly to oppose the tax. Brin’s campaign committee has also organised competing ballot propositions which, if passed, would nullify the tax.

For now, polling suggests the billionaire tax is supported by a majority of voters. More than 1.6 million Californians signed the petition to put the tax on the November ballot.

The future of wealth inequality

California’s coming election will serve as an important test of the political power of the billionaire class, and the broader health of American democracy.

Yet even if the tax is successful, taxing billionaires only treats a symptom of global inequality, rather than addressing its underlying causes.

A policy agenda for seriously addressing wealth inequality must also therefore include a much broader suite of measures. These might include improving workers’ bargaining power, breaking up monopolies and public ownership of AI technology.

Without these structural fixes, we should expect voter anger and the current political instability around the world to continue to escalate.

The result from the Jaws gold target included a blistering high-grade core of 7.62m grading an impressive 18.67g/t gold from 85.34m, with two individual 1.52-metre samples returning eye watering grades as high as 41g/t and 33.4g/t gold. It is also home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast, one of Canada’s largest gold mines. Manhattan’s standout drillhole represents a hefty upgrade on the nearest historic hole from the late 1980’s, which returned 22m at 2.41g/t gold. For some players, the prestige and/or location of a club is a big factor in their decision when it comes to transfers. After I left Germany, where I had limited opportunities, I decided I would never move to another club again without first speaking to the manager. Do they believe in me? Do they actually want me? How much will I play? I needed to hear it from them, in their words. Lucas Herrington will play for Hull City in the Premier League. Hull FC I would imagine Herrington and his representatives went through all of these questions. Look, it’s Barcelona; it’s a difficult one to turn down, and they weren’t the only big club after him. His progression so far has been phenomenal – which is exactly why you don’t want that progression to be stunted, and that was the risk. He should play a fair bit of football for Hull, who are back in the Premier League for the first time in a decade. title: Cameron Green blew up at a Shield game. It was the moment he turned his Test career around
text:

SportCricketAustralian cricket Cameron Green blew up at a Shield game. It was the moment he turned his Test career around Daniel Brettig August 20, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Cameron Green has revealed how a low moment last summer became the point at which he finally nailed down the formula to become the Test batter that Australia desperately need him to be. Green, 27, made unfortunate headlines in March when he got into a press conference confrontation with a journalist following a Sheffield Shield game in Sydney, but he said on Thursday that the hundred he made that day was the moment he committed to a red-ball batting method to take back to Test cricket. Cameron Green celebrates his century against Bangladesh in the first Test in Darwin. Getty Images The hundred had followed a frustrating Ashes summer where Green often looked in an inordinate rush to make things happen, summed up by an ugly dismissal, backing away and bowled by England’s Brydon Carse at the Gabba. Australia were humbled by Bangladesh in Darwin last week, but Green’s second-innings century was proof that the mode of batting he settled on in March – so much so that he is revisiting the notes he made on that innings – is the right one for him.

Advertisement

“I went back to how I used to play, just keeping it really simple,” Green said. “Over the last few years I’ve tinkered a bit more to find something, tried to force it a little bit, so it was nice to go back to Shield cricket for a game last year, just went back to what I used to do and it felt really good. “I got a bit of clarity after that Shield game. It’s easy when you can go back to what felt good and what has worked well in the past. That’s basically all I really did. Loading “I’d normally like to be reasonably front on, bat on middle stump, just a really clear, simple game plan. Over the previous few tours or years, trying to get to off stump, trying to play a slightly more aggressive game early, rather than letting it happen. I think that’s the unfortunate thing but also the fortunate thing that I have been through it.” Recalled opener Matt Renshaw took up position at first slip in training drills on Thursday morning, with Steve Smith at second and Green’s fellow all-rounder Beau Webster at third.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket ‘Why are you out to get me?’ Green’s dummy spit raises questions ahead of $4m IPL stint Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer Green’s homework is also a result of his struggles to balance the competing demands of three formats, and a reminder that while he is currently batting in Travis Head’s former position at No.5, he does not have to bat like the freewheeling South Australian to succeed. “Travis Head is an unbelievable cricketer, and he seems to be a guy who can hit shots from ball one,” Green said. “That’s never really been me, so it’s just going back to what feels right for me, what I’ve done my whole life, and it felt nice the other day. “You try and write down notes because it’s a long time since we played a red-ball game, so I tried to write down a few notes from what worked in that Shield game. We had a World Cup, IPL, and some one-dayers in between, so it’s nice to go back to what did work, and try to remind yourself of that. “When you’re trying to force it, you want to do really well when you’re playing for Australia, sometimes you try to force those results, and unfortunately, in Test cricket you can’t score a hundred within 10 overs, you have to bat a few hours to get there, and when you feel like you’re forcing it, you’re trying to rush it too quick, so trying to get into that tempo that does work.”

Advertisement

As a shy young man who loves the comforts of his home in Perth, Green has thought about how to handle the challenges of near constant travel over the next 12 months. In 2023, Green played well on a Test tour of India, notching his first Test century, but trailed off later in the year as homesickness and fatigue took hold. This time around, he is likely to be accompanied by his wife-to-be Emily and other family and friends at various stages of the calendar, the better to feel happy and grounded even when he's thousands of kilometres away from home. Cameron Green at work in the nets ahead of the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay. title: Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations
text:

InspirationGreat Ocean Road Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations Mex Cooper Updated August 20, 2026 — 11:09am ,first published August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s impossible to take the Great Ocean Road for granted: those sweeping ocean views at every twist and turn simply won’t let you. International travellers have made it Victoria’s most popular region for overnight stays, and Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements describes it as “one of Australia’s most compelling destinations”. But whether you’re crossing oceans to get here or you live close enough for a weekend getaway, it’s easy to stick to the same tourist stops. From off-grid retreats to sustainable dining, here are 10 ways to bypass the obvious and make travelling this spectacular stretch of bitumen a truly memorable experience. Get blown away Loch Ard Gorge lookout has stunning sights with fewer onlookers. The 12 Apostles rightly remain a must-see for tourists, even if there are only seven of the limestone pillars left. However, mere moments away, Loch Ard Gorge has similar stunning sights with fewer onlookers. Here you can delve into maritime history, including the famous shipwreck for which the gorge is named, before finding the blowhole lookout Poombeeyt Koontapool. Meaning “breath of the whale” in the Keerray Woorroong language, the elevated viewing platform allows you to hear the deep rumbles that precede crashing waves and the ocean whispers that carry calmer waters. Give the view time: watching it shift from serene to explosive can be mesmerising.

Advertisement

Sleep among the vines Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. A stay in the vineyard of Basalt Wines offers a snug cosy bedroom and stunning views. Two private villas set among the vines at boutique vineyard Basalt Wines (near Port Fairy), feel as luxurious as a 1920s boudoir with lush textiles and rich colours that entice you to curl up on the couch with a pinot noir. The only thing likely to draw you away is the cellar door restaurant, which pairs regional ingredients with Basalt’s own wines. Each villa has its own kitchenette, fireplace, deck, outside fire pit and breakfast hamper of local goodies. Killarney Beach and Tower Hill Wildlife Reserve are less than 10 minutes drive away. Wake to the ocean On clear nights, star gazing is unrivalled at Sky Pods.

Advertisement

Staying at Sky Pods makes you feel as if you have the edge of the ocean to yourself with 180-degree views across the Cape Otway coast. At dusk, a mob of grazing kangaroos hop into view before the sun sets over the Southern Ocean. Star gazing is unrivalled on clear nights but if too cloudy, a projector screen turns the luxury pod into a boutique cinema. This off-grid retreat, fed by solar power and filtered rain water, sits on 81 hectares of land being restored to its pre-farming state; 60,000 native trees have been planted over the past decade. A 20-minute walk down a bush track leads to Station Beach and access to the Great Ocean Walk, Aire River and Rainbow Falls. It’s a stay and view you will never forget. Meet the locals At Wildlife Wonders guides take groups through bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus and kangaroos. At Wildlife Wonders (five kilometres from Apollo Bay), expert guides take groups through protected bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus, kangaroos and many more. Visitors may be lucky enough to meet the rufous-bellied pademelon, a small wallaby-like marsupial that is extinct on the Australian mainland, or the even smaller long-nosed potoroo, while listening to the sounds of kookaburras, cockatoos and tree frogs. The 14-hectare sanctuary was established to raise funds for the Conservation Ecology Centre’s research projects. Dusk and dawn tours are available and in winter months there’s even a chance of spotting a migrating whale from the property’s commanding position. Feast from the sea

Advertisement

The Apollo Bay Fishing Co-op team with a fresh catch. No fancy five-star restaurant could compete with tucking into a freshly caught southern rock lobster at Apollo Bay’s Fishing Co-Operative. Since its establishment in 1948, the co-op has become a must for tourists and locals alike with its “ocean to plate” dining. The menu changes depending on the daily catch, but the true star is always there: grilled half rock lobster with garlic butter, chips and salad. The Apollo Bay harbour redevelopment shifted the co-op to a pop-up shop and separate fish market store, but both will reunite and return to their original and refurbished digs, including a new public viewing deck, by Christmas 2026. Go retro Angelsea’s The Monty sports a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. It’s only fitting that along one of the world’s best road trips, the classic roadside motel is being resurrected with a playful new vibe. Much like Australia’s original motor inns, Angelsea’s The Monty is inspired by American design, sporting a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. Mint-green walls, wavy mirrors, chequered bathrooms and bold orange accents bring the fun, while king-sized beds, curated mini-bars and coffee pod machines provide modern comforts. You can charge your EV or rent an electric bike. The lobby, which overlooks the Anglesea River, will morph into a new Mexican Cantina, Nina, to open in late 2026. It will feature a gluten-free menu with the right mix of sticky, tangy and fresh dishes with margaritas to match. The perfect spot to unwind after kayaking on the river or swimming at nearby beaches.

Advertisement

Ride a wave ... You may be surprised how far you go during a Go Ride a Wave surf lesson. Taking a surf lesson can feel daunting. There are the unpredictable waves, the ocean chill, the threat of rips, and the locals carving up the water, but halfway into a Go Ride A Wave two-hour class, and doubts begin to turn into a feeling you can do this. Some in your group may make it to standing, some to their knees, others stay flat, but most will likely leave surging with adrenaline and an urge to return. Supplied with a wetsuit, learner-friendly surfboard and plenty of expert guidance, the tutorial at famed Torquay beach is above all else exhilarating fun. … Then watch a pro Not a pro yet, but 13-year-old Leihani Zoric carves up a wave at Bells Beach’s Indigenous Surfing Titles in May. Justin McManus

Advertisement

Once you’ve realised just how tricky a pop-up can be, check out the masters at play as they weave through the waves at the Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach. The World Surf League Champion event, the longest running in competitive surfing, is held each Easter at the iconic beach. On days when the swell isn’t suitable, the action is halted but can provide the perfect opportunity to dive into Australia’s surfing culture and history at Torquay’s Australian National Surfing Museum. Enjoy a tasting tour Mediterranean-inspired deli Mortadeli serves sandwiches that demand your attention. Joe Armao The shared ingredient of the Great Ocean Road’s most delicious and diverse food is a commitment to quality seasonal produce. At the gateway to the road, the Booln Booln Cafe takes seemingly simple dishes such as sourdough jaffles and pastries and elevates them with native ingredients such as slow-cooked roo ragu and lemon myrtle meringue. At Aireys Inlet, cosy wine bar Le Comptoir invites you to while away hours grazing on a traditional French menu that incorporates local ingredients. Back in Torquay, Mortadeli, a Mediterranean-inspired deli and “caffeteria” serves seasonal soups, salads and pastas alongside its smash-hit sandwiches that demand both hands. Feed your soul

Advertisement

Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to charity. Bec Hudson And then there is one Surf Coast restaurant that is taking a really radical approach to sustainable dining. Torquay’s Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to local charity Feed Me, to help supply nutritious food to those in need. Using the food bank’s surplus vegetables, Samesyn transforms unwanted produce into critically acclaimed dishes, such as chewy carrots that are dehydrated then rehydrated in a carrot juice reduction and served with a maple sauce made from discarded Halloween pumpkins. There are no waiting staff, only chefs, who rotate through service shifts to share Samesyn’s mission – including achieving near zero waste – with customers. The nine-course tasting menu is a meal that will feed your soul. Related Article Great Ocean Road Australia’s wild and unforgiving coast makes this ‘great walk’ sublime THE DETAILS Visit

Wildlife Wonders offers a range of guided tours from $24-$75 for children and $59-$95 for adults. Family tickets and concessions available. See wildlifewonders.org.au. Go Ride A Wave in Torquay has two-hour surfing lessons for $84, wetsuit and surfboard hire included. See gorideawave.com.au/location/torquay. Admission to The Australian National Surfing Museum is between $8 and $25. See australiannationalsurfingmuseum.com.au; The Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach is on between March 25 and April 4, 2027.

Advertisement

Stay

An adults-only private villa at Basalt Retreat, including a breakfast hamper, is $495 a night with a two-night minimum stay Friday and Saturday. See basaltwines.com.au/stay. The adults-only Sky Pods are $485 a night for a minimum two-night stay. If you want one night’s accommodation, smaller Sky Ships can be booked for $420 a night. See skypods.com.au; rooms (king or twin) at The Monty from $120-$180 a night. See themontymotel.com.au The writer travelled as a guest of Visit Victoria.

The Australian sharemarket advanced in early trade on Thursday, tracking a recovery on Wall Street as pressure from the bond market eased after the US Treasury unveiled plans to buy back longer-dated debt to curb borrowing costs. Bloomberg Miners led the early gains, with gold miners rallying after bullion held the biggest gain in six months after the US Treasury’s surprise move to rein in long-term borrowing costs. The US Treasury unexpectedly announced it’s ramping up buybacks of long-dated government debt, signalling it wants to lower borrowing costs after yields hit multi-decade highs. Gold has been volatile in recent weeks amid fears Iran-war-fuelled inflation might force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which boosted bond yields and weighed non-yielding assets like gold. Northern Star Resources rallied 7 per cent, also after showing how it benefited from gold’s record highs earlier this year. Its net income soared 24 per cent to $1.7 billion in the year to June 30, the miner said, thanks to a 26 per cent rise in the average price it was able to fetch for its gold. The miner posted a net profit of $US2.9 billion for the 12 months to June 30, down 15 per cent on the year before. The results conclude a challenging year for Fortescue, which is in active negotiations with China’s state-backed iron ore buyer. China Mineral Resources Group has imposed restrictions on shipments of Super Special Fines, a cheaper low-grade ore that is one of Fortescue’s key exports. Its bigger rivals BHP and Rio Tinto gained in early trade, rising 2.5 per cent and 1.9 per cent, respectively.

Advertisement

Tech stocks were the other big winners, shrugging off falls by Big Tech stocks on Wall Street overnight. Software makers Xero and WiseTech - which slumped almost 9 per cent on Wednesday after the competition watchdog executed a search warrant on its offices - were up 2.6 per cent and 5.9 per cent. Communications and metal detection tech firm Codan soared 10.1 per cent after reporting a 69 per cent profit jump and raising its dividend by 70 per cent. Financial stocks were trading lower, with all big four banks down in early trade. CBA , Westpac and ANZ Bank shed 1.1 per cent each and National Australia Bank lost 1.2 per cent. Property giant Goodman Group slipped 1.2 per cent even after it said the boom in demand for data centres from AI and cloud computing, networking, and storage hyperscalers gave it a 15.7 per cent jump in full-year operating profit to $2.67 billion. “Automation and robotics continue to drive logistics requirements while scarcity of power and land remains the key constraint on AI and cloud growth supporting data centre demand,” chief executive Greg Goodman said. On Wall Street overnight, US stocks rose after the Treasury Department announced a move that could ease pressure coming from the bond market. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estée Lauder, Target and other US companies also helped support sentiment.

Advertisement

The S&P 500 climbed 0.2 per cent for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite ticked 0.2 per cent higher. Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Financial markets have come under growing strain as bond yields charged higher in recent months on worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors. That makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments. But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy.

Advertisement

Longer-term yields are set instead by investors in the bond market, who decide how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. The 30-year Treasury yield, which recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.18 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. The relief could be short-lived, some analysts warn, with the value of bonds the US Treasury is proposing to repurchase just a fraction of the overall total. “The boost to buybacks is also happening in a world of challenged Fed credibility,” according to strategists at BNP Paribas. Investors are questioning whether the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate soon to match the tough talk its chairman, Kevin Warsh, has been offering on getting inflation down toward its 2 per cent target.

title: No ego, no hierarchy, no boss: How to survive touring the world with your brother
text:
Advertisement

NationalGood Weekend No ego, no hierarchy, no boss: How to survive touring the world with your brother Katrina Strickland August 20, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dutch pianists Lucas Jussen, 33, and his brother, Arthur, 29, have been performing together since they were kids. Now regulars in the world’s top concert halls, they still share a room, and plates of food, on tour. Lucas (at front) and Arthur Jussen: “It’s very important that there’s not one boss,” says Arthur, “there must be a complete lack of ego in that way.” Marco Borggreve ARTHUR: Lucas is three-and-a-half years older than me, and when I came home from hospital, the first thing he did was hug and kiss me. That says something about the bond that was to develop; he accepted me straight away. He’s very easygoing and social, and I always played with Lucas and his friends when we were little. We slept in the same room, even though we each had our own; we could talk more. We still share a room when we’re on the road. We joke that if you go out with either one of us, you get the other brother, too. Thankfully, we like each other’s wives. Lucas has been with Annelise since he was 14, so I know her very well. I met my wife, Brenda, more recently. I’m a bit OCD. Lucas and Annelise bought an automatic vacuum cleaner and named it Arthur, so you can see how they mock me for that. I’m probably a bit square while Lucas is more spontaneous. If there was an important test, I’d start preparing a week before, whereas he’d do it all the day before. We’d end up in the same place, just via different methods.

Advertisement

Related Article Good Weekend At 14, Brett gave his sister a note and hid in the bathroom. Then she knocked on the door We really understand each other. One time, we were playing in Hamburg and, for some reason, I felt very nervous before going on stage. Lucas sensed this. Ten seconds before we went out, he said to me, “Look where we are; it’s amazing. Let’s enjoy it.” I instantly relaxed and we had a fantastic concert. Lucas had an especially busy year last year. He was moving house as well as performing a lot. I felt he was a little on edge, so I took on a lot of the admin that we usually share. I didn’t mind because I like to be organised and I knew it would just take something off his shoulders. We didn’t have to discuss it. We’re a very good team. If Lucas makes a joke on stage, I’m usually the first and loudest to laugh. What I find frustrating about him is also what I love. Lucas will give the receptionist or cleaning maid as much time as the boss; actually, he probably gives more to the maid. I really admire it but, sometimes, if you’re running late and he’s chatting for 10 minutes, you think, “C’mon!” But that’s just him; he’s very outgoing. We rehearse separately 90 per cent of the time and come together for the last 10 per cent. There’s no hierarchy when we play: it’s very important that there’s not one boss, there must be a complete lack of ego in that way. Every millisecond, I’m listening to what Lucas is doing and he’s doing the same, so who is leading can change within that millisecond.

Advertisement

When we’re sitting together [playing the same piano], I know when he wants to use one of the pedals, because I feel his leg gently touch mine. I know then to move mine away. That’s the easy thing about being brothers: you don’t have to bother saying, “When I touch your leg, it doesn’t mean I hate you.” We both like to work out and keep healthy and pretty much eat the same food; it’s not like one of us wants Chinese and the other Italian. We often get two plates of food, say a pasta and a salad, and share them. Even when it comes to music, we have the same tastes. We both like Frank Sinatra, Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder, Kool & the Gang, and Kylie Minogue. LUCAS: I can’t remember a time when I wasn’t with Arthur; I’d play more with him than with my own friends at school. We’ve asked our parents how we came to get along so well and they simply say, “It’s just luck; either you do or you don’t.” We certainly know siblings who really work on their relationships but don’t have the deep connection that we do. Arthur is a big dreamer – and I mean that in the literal sense. He’ll often have vivid dreams and talk in his sleep. One time, he woke me to tell me, “Calm down, calm down. It’s OK.” I woke up and said, “What’s the matter? I’m fine.” He looked me straight in the eye but he was fast asleep, probably dreaming.

Advertisement

Arthur likes to have structure in the way he approaches piano-playing and life; he likes to know what’s coming. He’ll be the one to fill in the visa forms. If a flight is delayed and we have to go on stage without a shower, I’d probably be easier about it than he would. I’ll be the one to say, “C’mon, it’ll be fine. We won’t smell as nice, but we’ll work it out.” The brothers have been performing together since they were children: “Every millisecond, I’m listening to what Lucas is doing and he’s doing the same,” Arthur says. @lucas_arthurjussen/instagram In terms of our looks, Arthur’s hair is more styled, whereas mine’s a bit wild. He’s more into fashion trends than I am, too: I tend to be a bit more classical. And he loves perfume. There’s a duty-free shop at Amsterdam airport with a huge fragrance section. We fly out of that airport two or three times a week and he would’ve been in that shop 300 times. He’s gone deep down the scent rabbit-hole and I don’t think he’s ever coming out. We spend more time apart from each other now that we’re both married. Last year, I spoke out because we’d done more than 100 concerts and I wanted to pull back on the intensity of that. Arthur wasn’t in the same headspace as me; he wanted to keep going. The difference [in what we wanted] was only small, but things came to a head. We talked it through, though, and met in the middle. He came to realise later that pulling back a bit had been good for him, too. I really admire Arthur’s drive to be the best he can be every time we go on stage together; he has a big tank in that way. It’s inspiring to have someone beside you who can deliver that drive all the time. If I’m having an off day, it pulls me through.
