title: ‘Bursting at the seams’: The schools that can’t keep up with student growth
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Bursting at the seams’: The schools that can’t keep up with student growth Jackson Graham and Craig Butt August 20, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Faith-based schools in Melbourne’s growth corridors are among the fastest-growing private educators in Victoria, with school leaders attributing the boom to parents favouring schools that reflect their religious values. Of the top 20 private schools that have recorded the biggest enrolment jumps over the past decade, more than half are faith-based – eight Islamic and five Christian – The Age’s analysis of enrolment data shows. Islamic schools such as Al Siraat College are among the fastest-growing private schools in Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Al Siraat College in Epping has grown by 911 students in the past 10 years – an increase of 142 per cent. Most of the school’s students were born in Australia, with their parents or grandparents migrating mostly from the Indian subcontinent or the Middle East. Collectively, the school’s families speak 39 languages other than English.

Advertisement

The expansion has brought growing pains, which deputy principal and co-founder, Rahat Arain, credits staff for managing “like a beautiful garden, growing”. “We are bursting at the seams, and trying to have our infrastructure play catch-up with the growth,” she said. “The pressures from the community wanting to enrol in an Islamic school have driven up the class sizes. That’s something that we then address through extra support staff in the classroom. This adds pressure to staffing to make sure that we have what’s required for a growing school population.” At school, all students learn Arabic and participate in prayers. Islamic teachings are also incorporated into the curriculum.

Advertisement

“For example, when we’re looking at civics and citizenship, you can look at it from a faith-based perspective as well,” Arain said. Al Siraat College co-founder and deputy principal Rahat Arain, who has seen the school grow by 900 students in the past decade. Ruby Alexander “What does our creator say about how we should be living a civic life? How does that compare to the opportunities we’ve got in Australia and democracy, and so forth. “Obviously, every school brings its own flavours, but I think our parents are looking for that overlay of how does it relate to who I am as a Muslim and how can [my child] access the curriculum?” The Australian International Academy of Education in Coburg – which opened in 1983 after a donation by then-king Khalid of Saudi Arabia and claims to be the oldest Islamic school in the country – has added 950 students in the past decade. The increase followed the opening of a new campus in Caroline Springs in 2014.

Advertisement

The Coburg campus, which has added 270 students in the past decade, recently opened a new multimillion-dollar building housing a prayer room and year 11 and 12 classrooms, and is nearing capacity, said campus head Michelle Shears. “Families are increasingly choosing faith-based schools because they are seeking an education that supports not only academic achievement, but also the development of strong character, values and a clear sense of identity,” Shears said. Many former students are now enrolling their own children at the school. “Their decision to return with subsequent generations demonstrates a level of trust and confidence that has been built over time,” Shears said. “Alongside new families joining our community, these generational connections contribute to our continued growth.”

The demographic picture is different at Heathdale Christian College, where most families are first-generation Australians, says executive principal Ross Grace. title: Forgot Book Week? Emergency costumes that require zero craft skills
text:
For some, Book Week is one of the most magical annual events in the Australian calendar – a time-honoured tradition stretching back generations (since 1945, specifically), where kids and their caregivers come together to get creative and celebrate their favourite stories and characters. For others, it’s just another tedious task that puts pressure on time-poor parents to whip up whimsy from their already-drained resources. Sometimes, it’s a bit of both.

There’s no doubt that, as with many other things, the rise of social media has seen the expectations around Book Week costumes soar, with the twin thieves of joy – competition and comparison – leading many parents to want to give up altogether or worse, pull out the Elsa and Woody costumes from the bottom of the dress-up box and call it a day.

The point of Book Week is, of course, to put books front and centre, and the costume frenzy can sometimes cause that to get lost. Because as much as kids might want to be a Disney princess or K-Pop Demon Hunter, it defeats the purpose (unless, of course, their primary point of contact for those characters is the book versions – in which case, break out the purple braids!).

It’s hard to keep up with the never-ending homework assignments of parenthood. But Book Week is a great opportunity to take a moment to connect with kids if you let the books lead the way, rather than the costumes. Going to the library or your home bookshelves and combing through them with your kids, having conversations about their favourite stories and characters, is far more important than any elaborately styled outfit.

Then, when it comes to the actual dressing up, it doesn’t have to be complicated. Adapting everyday clothing and household items you already own can be part of the fun – and online hubs like Facebook Marketplace are a great additional way to simplify the process, whether that’s by finding completed costumes that are being offloaded from Book Weeks past, or reusable items and materials you need to complete your kids’ looks.

When was the last time you sat down at a bar and ordered a glass of Japanese wine? Not rice wine, but a rosé pét-nat from Nagano, say, or a cabernet sauvignon-merlot blend from Miyagi?

These are just some of the wines on offer at Aenza, a Japanese wine bar in Darlinghurst from the team behind Amuro. The drinks list, curated by beverage manager Paul Beaton (formerly head sommelier at Aria), focuses on wines from Australia, France and Japan. There are more than 120 bottles on offer, 38 of them by the glass. Beyond wine, there’s Japanese whisky, gin, sake, shochu and umeshu, plus five highball cocktails to choose from.

The food menu, by owner and chef Joy Liu, focuses on Australian-Japanese snacks, and includes red emperor sashimi with mandarin ponzu, eggplant agebitashi and karaage chicken with takana (mustard greens) mayo.

title: Costco store praised for kind act helping thousands of Aussies doing it tough
text:
A Costco store has been praised for a simple act helping thousands of Australians doing it tough — donating surplus meat and other food to a Queensland charity rather than letting it go to waste.

Costco North Lakes, in Brisbane's north, has been supporting Nourish Street for more than a year, with meat approaching its use-by date frozen and handed over to the organisation to help prepare meals for people experiencing homelessness and financial hardship.

Nourish Street founder and president Beau Haywood said the supermarket's support had made a significant difference, with the donated food going well beyond the charity's own meal programs.

"They take it off the shelf, throw it in their freezer for us," Beau told Yahoo News.

"We pick it up and put it in ours."

The meat is then distributed to community groups and businesses that use the protein to prepare meals, meaning a donation from one Costco store can ultimately reach thousands of people across the wider community.

Food going beyond one charity

Nourish Street prepares around 850 meals each week through its own programs, but Beau said the organisation uses only about 30 per cent of the meat it receives.

The rest is passed on to other community groups, including those running soup kitchens and other meal programs.

"And the rest of it, we actually pass on to other community groups."

"Food should be, as much as possible, if it's safe and still fit for human consumption, passed on to community groups and people that are really feeling the pinch," he said.
